It tempts because victories are often read as the win of the bigger army. Remember: Plassey was won by Mir Jafar's inaction, not by numbers.

qs.q:
Read the following passage. A Mughal province, the suba, had a governor and a provincial diwan. The provincial diwan answered to the imperial diwan and not to the governor, so that the governor did not hold both the sword and the purse. In order of size the units run pargana, then sarkar, then suba. On the basis of this passage, consider the following conclusions:
1. A sarkar was a smaller unit than a pargana.
2. A suba lay wholly inside one sarkar.
3. The provincial diwan was a subordinate of the governor of the suba.
Which one of the following conclusions, based on the above statements, is correct?
o: There are two correct statements that include statement 1.
There is only one correct statement.
qs.e: There is no correct statement. The passage orders the units pargana, sarkar, suba, so a pargana is smaller than a sarkar, and a sarkar, not a suba, is the unit that sits inside a larger one. The provincial diwan answered to the imperial diwan, not to the governor, which is the check that separated the sword from the purse. The first two tempt by turning the order round. Remember: pargana, sarkar, suba, from small to large.

qs.q:
Read the following passage. Scholars place Nimbarka, the Dvaitadvaita acharya, anywhere from the 7th to the 14th century, and no reference makes him a contemporary of Akbar. Jaswant Singh of Marwar died in 1678, and Aurangzeb took over Marwar in 1679. Durgadas saved the infant Ajit Singh, and Prince Akbar sided with the Rajputs. Ahadis were gentlemen troopers who served directly under the emperor, not under any noble. On the basis of this passage, consider the following conclusions:
1. Even the latest date proposed for Nimbarka falls before the 16th century in which Akbar ruled.
2. Aurangzeb took over Marwar in the year after the death of Jaswant Singh.
3. An ahadi was not a retainer of any noble.
Which one of the following conclusions, based on the above statements, is correct?
o: There are two correct statements that include statement 1.
There is only one correct statement.
qs.e: All three statements are correct. The latest date proposed for Nimbarka, the 14th century, is earlier than Akbar's 16th, which matches the passage that no reference makes them contemporaries. Jaswant Singh died in 1678 and Aurangzeb took over Marwar in 1679, the following year. Ahadis served directly under the emperor, so they were not a noble's men. Prince Akbar in the passage is a different person from the emperor Akbar and tempts a wrong link. Remember: Nimbarka is not Akbar's contemporary, and ahadis served the emperor alone.

qs.q:
Consider the following statements about Deva Raya II of Vijayanagara:
1. He was known as Gajabetekara, the hunter of elephants.
2. He fought the Gajapati rulers of Orissa in several rounds.
3. He ruled from c. 1423 to 1446.
4. He was the first ruler of the Saluva dynasty.
How many of the above statements are correct?
qs.e: Three statements are correct. Deva Raya II, who ruled c. 1423 to 1446, was called Gajabetekara and fought the Gajapati rulers of Orissa in several rounds. Statement 4 fails because he belonged to the Sangama line; the first Saluva was Saluva Narasimha, who came in 1485. The title tempts a later-dynasty label because his fame was great. Remember: Deva Raya II is Sangama; Saluva Narasimha opens the Saluvas.

qs.q:
Consider the following statements about Firuz Shah Tughlaq:
Statement I: Under Firuz Shah Tughlaq iqtas became effectively hereditary.
Statement II: Firuz Shah set up the Diwan-i-Bandagan, a department for slaves, whom he employed as bodyguards and craftsmen.
Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements?
o: Both Statement I and Statement II are correct and Statement II explains Statement I
Both Statement I and Statement II are correct and Statement II does not explain Statement I
Statement I is correct but Statement II is not correct
Statement I is not correct but Statement II is correct
qs.e: Both statements are correct, but Statement II does not explain Statement I. Iqtas became effectively hereditary under Firuz, which weakened the centre, while the Diwan-i-Bandagan was a separate reform for slaves. Slave bodyguards and craftsmen did not make iqtas pass from father to son. The link tempts because both measures are listed among the causes of a weak centre. Remember: hereditary iqtas and the slave department are two reforms, not one chain.

qs.q:
Consider the following statements about the literature of Vijayanagara:
1. Krishnadevaraya of the Tuluva dynasty wrote the Amuktamalyada in Telugu, a work on kingship.
2. Allasani Peddana, the foremost of the Ashtadiggajas, wrote the Telugu work Manucharitamu.
3. The Amuktamalyada advises the king to improve harbours so that horses, elephants and gems can be freely exported.
How many of the above statements are correct?
qs.e: Only two statements are correct. Krishnadevaraya wrote the Amuktamalyada in Telugu, and Allasani Peddana, foremost of the Ashtadiggajas, wrote the Manucharitamu. Statement 3 reverses the flow of trade: the king is advised to improve harbours so that horses, elephants and gems come in freely, not go out. Export tempts because harbours are linked with sale abroad. Remember: harbours improved to bring horses and gems in.

qs.q:
Consider the following statements:
1. The Third Battle of Panipat, fought on 14 January 1761, ended in a complete Afghan victory over the Marathas.
2. The Second Battle of Panipat, in 1556, was fought between Babur and Ibrahim Lodi.
3. At Panipat in 1761 the Marathas under Sadashiv Rao Bhau faced Ahmad Shah Abdali.
4. In the Mughal grading of land, parauti was land left fallow for three to four years.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
qs.e: Statements 1 and 3 are correct. The Marathas under Sadashiv Rao Bhau met Ahmad Shah Abdali on 14 January 1761, and the Afghans won completely. Statement 2 gives the First Battle of 1526 to the Second; in 1556 Hemu faced Akbar's side under Bairam Khan. Statement 4 swaps land grades: chachar lay fallow three to four years, parauti for a time. Both lures tempt because the names are close. Remember: 1526 Babur, 1556 Hemu, 1761 Abdali; chachar three to four years.

qs.q:
Consider the following statements about Fa-hien:
1. He was a Chinese Buddhist monk who visited India in the reign of Chandragupta II.
2. His book is the Foguoji, the Record of Buddhist Kingdoms.
3. His journey is given as 399 to 412 CE, a convention.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
qs.e: All three statements are correct. Fa-hien, a Chinese Buddhist monk, came in the reign of Chandragupta II and wrote the Foguoji, the Record of Buddhist Kingdoms. His journey is given as 399 to 412 CE by convention. A doubt may arise because Hiuen Tsang is the better-known Chinese monk, but his period is the reign of Harsha. Remember: Fa-hien with Chandragupta II; Hiuen Tsang with Harsha.

qs.q: Which one of the following statements about the monasteries of the Pala age is correct?
o: Devapala founded Vikramashila in Bihar, and Dharmapala later restored it.
Dharmapala founded the monastery of Nalanda and took Haribhadra as his spiritual guide.
Devapala founded the monastery of Nalanda, which Dharmapala later restored.
Dharmapala founded Vikramashila and Somapura, while Nalanda was far older.
qs.e: The last choice is correct: Dharmapala founded Vikramashila and Somapura Mahavihara, and Nalanda was far older, though the Palas backed it. The first gives the founding of Vikramashila to Devapala, and the third gives Nalanda to him, though it was founded long before the Palas. The second makes Dharmapala the founder of Nalanda, which is equally wrong. The Pala names are easy to swap because the father and son are both great patrons. Remember: Dharmapala founded Vikramashila and Somapura; Nalanda was already old.

qs.q:
Consider the following pairs of a person or order and a fact:
1. Naqshbandi order : Reached India with the invasion of Babur
2. Ahmad Sirhindi : Opposed Akbar's mixing policies and was jailed by Jahangir
3. Shah Waliullah : An 18th-century Naqshbandi
4. Khwaja Baqi Billah : Brought the Naqshbandi order to India in the time of Sher Shah, who rebuilt the Grand Trunk Road
How many of the above pairs are correctly matched?
qs.e: Only two pairs are correctly matched. Ahmad Sirhindi opposed Akbar's syncretic policies and Jahangir jailed him, and Shah Waliullah was an 18th-century Naqshbandi. The order did not enter India with Babur; Khwaja Baqi Billah brought it late in the 16th century, long after Sher Shah, who ruled for five years from 1540. Both wrong pairs tempt by placing the order too early. Remember: Baqi Billah, late 16th century, then Sirhindi.

qs.q:
Consider the following statements about the Paramaras:
1. The Paramaras ruled Malwa.
2. Upendra (Krishnaraja), not Siyaka, was the first independent Paramara king.
3. Siyaka was the first independent Paramara king, known from a plate of 949.
4. Dhara replaced Mandu as the Paramara capital at a later time.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
qs.e: Statements 1 and 3 are correct. The Paramaras ruled Malwa, and Siyaka is their first independent king, known from the Harsola plate of 949. Statement 2 fails because Siyaka, not Upendra, was the first independent king; Upendra appears in later lists and historians doubt him as a founder. Statement 4 reverses the capitals: Dhara came first and Mandu replaced it. Upendra tempts because later lists name him first. Remember: Siyaka first independent king; Dhara, then Mandu.

qs.q: Which one of the following statements about Bahlul Lodi is correct?
o: He placed his son Sikandar on the Jaunpur throne in 1486 after finally defeating the Sharqis in battle.
He founded the Sayyid dynasty, which was the first Afghan dynasty of the Sultanate, in 1414.
He fought the Sharqi sultans for years and was killed at Panipat in 1526 by Babur, the first Mughal.
He founded the first Afghan dynasty and placed his son Barbak at Jaunpur in 1486.
qs.e: The last choice is correct: Bahlul Lodi, who ruled from 1451 to 1489, founded the Lodis, the first Afghan dynasty of the Sultanate, and placed Barbak on the Jaunpur throne in 1486 after long wars with the Sharqis. Sikandar was his successor at Delhi, not the Jaunpur ruler. The Sayyids were an earlier line, and Ibrahim Lodi, not Bahlul, was killed at Panipat in 1526. Remember: Bahlul and Barbak at Jaunpur; Ibrahim fell at Panipat.

qs.q:
Consider the following pairs of a Chinese monk and a fact:
1. Hiuen Tsang : Wrote the Si-yu-ki, Records of the Western Regions, finished in 646
2. Hiuen Tsang : Travelled in India in the reign of Harsha and studied at Nalanda
3. Hiuen Tsang : Left India by sea from Tamralipti and spent about two years in Sri Lanka
4. I-tsing : Left in 671 by sea and spent about ten years at Nalanda
How many of the above pairs are correctly matched?
qs.e: Three pairs are correctly matched. Hiuen Tsang wrote the Si-yu-ki, finished in 646, and travelled in India under Harsha, studying at Nalanda; I-tsing sailed in 671 and spent about ten years at Nalanda. Leaving from Tamralipti by sea and spending two years in Sri Lanka is Fa-hien's journey; Hiuen Tsang went home overland. The lure is that all three were Chinese monks. Remember: Fa-hien with Chandragupta II, Hiuen Tsang with Harsha, I- tsing by sea.

qs.q:
Consider the following statements about the label "early medieval" and the age that followed:
1. It is a label by convention, used for about the 7th to the 12th century.
2. In that age power moved from one empire to many regional courts.
3. Ghazi Malik took the name Ghiyasuddin Tughlaq and began Tughlaqabad in the early 14th century, which falls after the age the label covers.
4. In the Sultanate that followed, jizya was a tax on Muslims and zakat a tax on non-Muslims.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
qs.e: Statements 1, 2 and 3 are correct. The label is a convention for about the 7th to the 12th century, when power moved from one empire to many regional courts, and Tughlaqabad belongs to the 14th century, after that age. Statement 4 swaps the taxes: zakat was a charity tax on Muslims and jizya a tax on non-Muslims. It tempts because both are religious taxes of the Islamic scheme. Remember: zakat for Muslims, jizya for non-Muslims.

qs.q:
Read the following passage. Vatsaraja, the Pratihara king, defeated Indrayudha of Kannauj and then Dharmapala. Dhruva, the Rashtrakuta, struck Vatsaraja down. Dhruva also beat Dharmapala in the Doab, but took no land and went back south. Dharmapala then took Kannauj and set up Chakrayudha as a vassal. Govinda III crushed the Pratihara Nagabhata, and both Chakrayudha and Dharmapala bowed to him. After Govinda III died, Nagabhata II took Kannauj and made it the Pratihara capital. On the basis of this passage, consider the following conclusions:
1. Dhruva struck Vatsaraja down before Dharmapala took Kannauj.
2. Chakrayudha was set up as a vassal after Nagabhata II had taken Kannauj.
3. Dhruva's victory over Dharmapala brought the Doab under lasting Rashtrakuta rule.
Which one of the following conclusions, based on the above statements, is correct?
o: There are two correct statements that include statement 1.
There is only one correct statement.
qs.e: There is only one correct statement, statement 1. The order runs Vatsaraja, Dhruva, Dharmapala at Kannauj with Chakrayudha, Govinda III, then Nagabhata II. Statement 2 reverses it, since Nagabhata II took Kannauj after Chakrayudha was installed and after Govinda III died. Statement 3 fails because Dhruva took no land and returned south. The lure is that raids look like conquests. Remember: Dhruva raided and went home; Nagabhata II took Kannauj last.

qs.q:
Consider the following statements about the reign of Jahangir:
1. Shah Jahan married Mehr-un-Nissa, called Nur Jahan, who gained great political influence at court.
2. Jahangir married Mehr-un-Nissa, called Nur Jahan, in 1611, and she gained great political influence at court.
3. Jahangir kept a Chain of Justice for direct appeals, and his memoir is the Padshahnama.
How many of the above statements are correct?
qs.e: Only one statement is correct, statement 2. Jahangir married Mehr-un-Nissa, Nur Jahan, in 1611, and she gained great influence. Statement 1 gives her to Shah Jahan, and statement 3 gives Jahangir the Padshahnama, which Abdul Hamid Lahori wrote for Shah Jahan; Jahangir's memoir is the Tuzuk-i-Jahangiri. Both tempt because father and son and their court books are easily mixed. Remember: Jahangir with Nur Jahan and the Tuzuk.

qs.q:
Consider the following statements about the later Mughal emperors:
1. Bahadur Shah I was followed by Jahandar Shah and then by Farrukhsiyar.
2. Nadir Shah's raid of 1739 fell in the reign of Muhammad Shah.
3. Alamgir II came to the throne before Ahmad Shah Bahadur.
4. The Battle of Plassey in 1757 fell in the reign of Alamgir II.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
qs.e: Statements 1, 2 and 4 are correct. After Bahadur Shah I came Jahandar Shah and Farrukhsiyar; Muhammad Shah, who reigned 1719 to 1748, was on the throne at Nadir Shah's raid of 1739; Alamgir II reigned 1754 to 1759, which covers Plassey in 1757. Statement 3 reverses the last two, since Ahmad Shah Bahadur ruled first. The names sound alike, which is the lure. Remember: Muhammad Shah, Ahmad Shah Bahadur, Alamgir II, in that order.

qs.q:
With reference to air pollutants, consider the following statements:
1. Ground-level ozone is a primary pollutant, because vehicle exhaust releases it directly into the air.
2. A secondary pollutant is not released as such; it forms in the air when primary pollutants react.
3. Peroxyacetyl nitrate (PAN), formed from nitrogen oxides and hydrocarbons, is a secondary pollutant.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
qs.e: Statements 2 and 3 are correct. A primary pollutant enters the air in the form in which it was released, while a secondary pollutant is made in the air from primary ones; PAN, built from nitrogen oxides and hydrocarbons, is a standard example. Statement 1 fails on "primary": no exhaust pipe emits ozone, which forms when nitrogen oxides and volatile organic compounds react in sunlight. It tempts because traffic is indeed the origin of those ingredients. Hook: primary pollutants are emitted, secondary pollutants are assembled in the air.

qs.q:
With reference to the two main kinds of smog, consider the following statements:
1. Sulphurous smog is tied to the burning of coal and other sulphur-rich fuels and is made worse by damp air.
2. Photochemical smog builds up best on cold, foggy nights, since its ingredients react only in the absence of sunlight.
3. A region that burns much coal but has little traffic is more at risk of photochemical smog than of sulphurous smog.
Which one of the following conclusions, based on the above statements, is correct?
o: There are two correct statements that include statement 1.
There is only one correct statement.
qs.e: Only statement 1 is correct. Sulphurous (London) smog comes from coal smoke and thickens in damp air. Statement 2 fails on "absence of sunlight": photochemical (Los Angeles) smog is made when nitrogen oxides and hydrocarbons react in strong sunlight. Statement 3 hands the coal region the wrong smog: coal smoke and sulphur oxides point to sulphurous smog, while photochemical smog depends chiefly on traffic exhaust and strong sun. Statement 2 tempts because the word smog suggests fog and smoke for every kind. Hook: London smog is coal, sulphur and damp; Los Angeles smog is traffic, sunlight and ozone.

qs.q: On calm, clear winter nights the air close to the ground in a landlocked city turns colder than the air a few hundred metres above it. Smoke from evening fires then hangs over the city until late the next morning. Which one of the following best explains why the smoke does not disperse?
o: The cold surface air is denser than the warm air above it, so it cannot rise and carry the smoke away.
Cold air holds very little water vapour, so no rain forms to wash the smoke particles out of the air.
The warm layer above is heavier than the cold air below it, so it sinks and presses the smoke downward.
Low temperature slows the chemical reactions by which the atmosphere breaks smoke down into gases.
qs.e: This is a temperature inversion. Normally air cools with height, so warm surface air rises and carries pollutants up. When the surface air is the colder and denser layer, it stays put under the warm layer, which acts as a lid, and smoke collects below it until the sun warms the ground. The third option tempts because it also speaks of a warm layer above, but warm air is lighter and does not sink. Hook: in an inversion, warm air sits over cold air, mixing stops and pollutants stay near the ground.

qs.q:
Consider the following statements about acid rain:
1. Rain falling through unpolluted air is neutral; it becomes acidic only where the air is polluted.
2. The acids can reach the ground even in dry weather, by settling on surfaces with dust and smoke.
3. Soils that are alkaline can neutralise part of the acid, so they are harmed less than soils that lack this buffering capacity.
How many of the above statements are correct?
qs.e: Only two statements are correct, 2 and 3. Acids formed from sulphur dioxide and nitrogen oxides come down with rain, snow or fog (wet deposition) and also settle with dust and gases in dry weather (dry deposition). Alkaline soils buffer the acid and suffer less. Statement 1 fails on "neutral": carbon dioxide dissolves in rain as weak carbonic acid, so even clean rain is slightly acidic. It tempts because pure water is neutral. Hook: carbon dioxide makes rain mildly acidic; sulphur and nitrogen oxides make it acid rain.

qs.q:
Consider the following statements:
1. Ozone near the ground is a different gas from the ozone of the stratosphere, which is why the first harms living things while the second protects them.
2. Ground-level ozone usually reaches its highest levels at night, because sunlight destroys it during the day.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
qs.e: Neither statement is correct. Statement 1 fails on "different gas": ozone is one gas, which screens out ultraviolet rays in the stratosphere and harms lungs and crops near the ground; the place, not the substance, differs. Statement 2 reverses the role of sunlight: ground-level ozone forms when nitrogen oxides and volatile organic compounds react in sunlight, so it peaks on sunny days. Statement 1 tempts because the two effects are opposite, statement 2 because ultraviolet light does break ozone high up. Hook: ozone is good up high and bad nearby, and at ground level sunshine makes it.

qs.q:
With reference to the Antarctic ozone hole, consider the following statements:
1. Polar stratospheric clouds provide the surfaces on which stable chlorine compounds are changed into reactive forms.
2. Ozone loss is at its fastest in the middle of the polar winter, because the reactions that destroy ozone need darkness.
3. A comparable hole is rarer over the Arctic, because the polar vortex there is weaker and the stratosphere warmer.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
qs.e: Statements 1 and 3 are correct. Inside the cold winter vortex, polar stratospheric clouds form, and on their surfaces stable "reservoir" chlorine compounds are turned into reactive chlorine. The warmer Arctic stratosphere and its weaker vortex make such clouds, and so a deep hole, less common there. Statement 2 fails on "darkness": the winter only prepares the chlorine, and ozone is destroyed fastest when sunlight returns in spring. It tempts because the clouds themselves are a winter feature. Hook: winter loads the gun, spring sunlight fires it (the chemistry behind the Montreal Protocol).

qs.q:
Consider the following statements:
Statement I: The Kigali Amendment brought hydrofluorocarbons (HFCs) under the Montreal Protocol, although HFCs do not deplete the ozone layer.
Statement II: HFCs, which came into wide use as substitutes for ozone-depleting substances, are powerful greenhouse gases.
Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements?
o: Both Statement I and Statement II are correct and Statement II explains Statement I
Both Statement I and Statement II are correct and Statement II does not explain Statement I
Statement I is correct but Statement II is not correct
Statement I is not correct but Statement II is correct
qs.e: Both statements are correct and Statement II explains Statement I. HFCs contain no chlorine or bromine, so they do not harm ozone, but they trap heat strongly, and their use grew precisely because the Montreal Protocol phased out the older gases. The Protocol therefore took charge of a climate problem that its own success had created. The second option tempts readers who think an ozone treaty can deal only with ozone- depleting gases. Hook: CFCs harm ozone and climate, HFCs harm climate alone, and the Kigali Amendment phases them down.

qs.q:
Consider the following pairs of pollution-control devices and the way each one works:
1. Electrostatic precipitator : Gives dust particles an electric charge and collects them on plates
2. Wet scrubber : Uses a liquid to trap particles and gases such as sulphur dioxide
3. Catalytic converter : Holds back soot from vehicle exhaust in fabric bags Which of the pairs given above is/are correctly matched?
qs.e: Pairs 1 and 2 are correctly matched. An electrostatic precipitator charges dust particles and collects them on earthed plates, and a wet scrubber passes the gas through a liquid that captures particles and soluble gases such as sulphur dioxide. Pair 3 borrows the working of a fabric (baghouse) filter. A catalytic converter traps nothing: its metal catalyst changes carbon monoxide, unburnt hydrocarbons and nitrogen oxides into less harmful gases. It tempts because both devices clean exhaust. Hook: precipitators and filters remove particles, scrubbers wash gases, converters convert them.

qs.q: Which one of the following best explains why ocean acidification harms corals and shell-forming plankton?
o: Sea water has turned more acidic than rain water, so shells dissolve as fast as they form.
Dissolved carbon dioxide pushes oxygen out of sea water, so these organisms suffocate.
More acidic water lets less sunlight through, so the algae living inside them cannot grow.
The added carbon dioxide leaves fewer carbonate ions for building calcium carbonate.
qs.e: Carbon dioxide dissolving in sea water forms carbonic acid, which releases hydrogen ions; these combine with carbonate ions, leaving fewer for corals and calcareous plankton to build calcium carbonate shells and skeletons. The first option tempts because of the word "acidification", but sea water is still alkaline, with a pH above 7; it is only becoming less alkaline. The process has nothing to do with oxygen being displaced or with light being blocked. Hook: more carbon dioxide means more hydrogen ions and fewer carbonate ions, which is why it is called "the other carbon dioxide problem".

qs.q:
With reference to black carbon (soot), consider the following statements:
1. It stays in the air for a short time only, so a cut in its emissions reduces its warming effect quickly.
2. When it settles on snow and ice it darkens the surface, which then reflects less sunlight and melts faster.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
qs.e: Both statements are correct. Black carbon is a particle produced by incomplete burning, not a gas; it absorbs sunlight strongly and warms the air, but rain and snow wash it out within days to weeks, so its warming fades soon after emissions stop. On snow and ice it lowers albedo, the share of sunlight reflected, and hastens melting. Statement 1 may look doubtful to those who expect every warming agent to linger as carbon dioxide does. Hook: black carbon is a short-lived climate pollutant, strong while it lasts and quick to clear.

qs.q:
With reference to measures of water pollution, consider the following statements:
1. A rise in the biochemical oxygen demand (BOD) of a river stretch generally goes with a fall in its dissolved oxygen.
2. For the same sample, chemical oxygen demand (COD) is normally lower than BOD, because COD leaves out the biodegradable matter.
3. An effluent rich in organic compounds that microbes cannot digest may show a modest BOD and yet a high COD.
Which one of the following conclusions, based on the above statements, is correct?
o: There are two correct statements that include statement 3.
There is only one correct statement.
qs.e: Two statements are correct, 1 and 3. BOD is the oxygen that microbes need to break down the organic waste in water, so a high BOD means much waste and a falling stock of dissolved oxygen. COD is the oxygen needed to oxidise all oxidisable matter chemically, digestible or not; it is therefore normally the higher figure, and statement 2 reverses this. It tempts because COD sounds like the narrower, chemical test. An effluent of non- biodegradable organics thus shows a modest BOD and a high COD. Hook: BOD counts what microbes can eat, COD counts everything that can be oxidised.

qs.q: Which one of the following is a non-point source of water pollution?
o: A drainpipe carrying effluent from a tannery into a river
The outfall of a city sewage treatment plant
Fertiliser washed off farmland across a river basin by rain
A channel returning cooling water from a power plant
qs.e: Fertiliser washed off farmland is a non-point source: the pollution enters the river from a wide area through runoff, with no single outlet. A drainpipe, an outfall and a discharge channel are each one identifiable outlet, that is, point sources, which can be treated or regulated at the pipe. The sewage outfall tempts because it gathers waste from a whole city, but it still reaches the river at one place. Hook: a point source has an address and can be regulated there; a non-point source is spread over the land and is far harder to control.

qs.q:
With reference to eutrophication of a lake, consider the following statements:
1. Nitrates and phosphates harm the lake mainly by poisoning its fish directly.
2. A thick surface bloom of algae cuts off light from the plants growing below it.
3. The decay of dead algae and plants by microbes uses up the oxygen dissolved in the water.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
qs.e: Statements 2 and 3 are correct. Nitrates and phosphates are plant nutrients; they feed a burst of algae at the surface. The bloom shades the submerged plants, which die, and microbes decomposing the dead plants and algae consume the dissolved oxygen until fish suffocate. Statement 1 fails on "poisoning": the nutrients fertilise the water, and the damage is done indirectly through loss of oxygen. It tempts because fish kills are the visible result. Hook, in sequence: nutrients, bloom, shade, decay, oxygen loss, dead zone.

qs.q:
Consider the following statements:
Statement I: Releasing heated cooling water from a power plant into a river raises the amount of oxygen dissolved in the river water.
Statement II: Water holds less dissolved gas as its temperature rises.
Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements?
o: Both Statement I and Statement II are correct and Statement II explains Statement I
Both Statement I and Statement II are correct and Statement II does not explain Statement I
Statement I is correct but Statement II is not correct
Statement I is not correct but Statement II is correct
qs.e: Statement I is not correct but Statement II is correct. Gases dissolve less in warm water than in cold, so a discharge of heated cooling water lowers the dissolved oxygen of the river, and fish accustomed to steady temperatures are harmed although no toxic substance has been added. This is thermal pollution. Statement I tempts those who think of warmth as favourable to life and overlook what it does to dissolved oxygen. Hook: warm water holds less oxygen, which is why heat alone counts as a water pollutant.

qs.q:
A plot of land is contaminated both with spilled diesel and with cadmium, and soil microbes are to be used to clean it. With reference to this plan, consider the following statements:
1. The microbes can be expected to break the diesel down into simpler, less harmful substances.
2. The microbes can be expected to break the cadmium down into harmless substances in the same way.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
qs.e: Only statement 1 is correct. Bioremediation works on biodegradable compounds: microbes use the hydrocarbons of diesel as food and break them into simpler, less toxic products. Cadmium is an element, so there is nothing for microbes to break it into; a heavy metal can only be changed in chemical form, held in place or taken up, for instance by plants that are then harvested. Statement 2 tempts because bioremediation is often described as a general cleaner of polluted soil. Hook: compounds can be degraded, elements cannot.

qs.q:
With reference to the treatment of water for drinking, consider the following statements:
1. A coagulant makes fine suspended particles clump together so that they can settle out.
2. Chlorine continues to protect water inside the supply pipes, because a small residual dose remains in it.
3. Ozone is the better choice for long-lasting protection along the pipe network, because it stays in water longer than chlorine.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
qs.e: Statements 1 and 2 are correct. A coagulant such as alum makes fine particles clump into flocs that sink in the sedimentation tank, and chlorine leaves a residual dose that goes on killing germs in the pipes. Statement 3 reverses the comparison: ozone is a strong disinfectant but is unstable and leaves no residue, so it cannot guard water on its way to the tap. It tempts because ozone leaves no taste or smell and seems the superior choice. Hook: ozone disinfects at the plant, while residual chlorine protects the water all the way to the tap.

qs.q:
With reference to the management of waste, consider the following statements:
1. In the waste hierarchy, burning waste to recover energy ranks above recycling it.
2. A circular economy aims to keep materials in use through repair, reuse and recycling.
3. The waste hierarchy treats safe disposal as the first choice and prevention as the last resort.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
qs.e: Only statement 2 is correct. A circular economy keeps materials in use by reuse, repair, refurbishing and recycling, unlike the linear "take, make, waste" model. The waste hierarchy runs from prevention and minimisation through reuse, recycling and recovery to safe disposal as the last resort. Statement 1 puts energy recovery above recycling, and statement 3 turns the whole order upside down. Statement 1 tempts because recovering energy sounds like the fullest use of waste, yet it destroys the material. Hook: prevent, minimise, reuse, recycle, recover, dispose, in that order.

qs.q: Which one of the following best describes Extended Producer Responsibility (EPR)?
o: The consumer pays a disposal charge to the local body each time a product is thrown away.
The local body must collect and recycle packaging waste at the cost of the general taxpayer.
The producer stays answerable for its product after use and must arrange or pay for recycling.
The recycler must pay the producer for the materials recovered from its discarded products.
qs.e: Extended Producer Responsibility makes the producer answerable for the environmentally sound management of its product until the end of its life, so the producer, importer or brand owner must arrange collection and recycling or pay for it. The first option tempts because the consumer is the one who discards the product, but EPR deliberately moves the duty back to the firm that designed and sold it. It does not rest on the local body or the recycler. Hook: EPR applies the polluter pays principle to products, and India's rules on plastic, e-waste and batteries are built on it.

qs.q:
Consider the following statements about hazardous waste:
1. A waste that is not poisonous can still be hazardous if it catches fire easily or is corrosive.
2. A waste that is toxic but is not ignitable, corrosive or reactive falls outside the definition of hazardous waste.
3. A reactive waste is one that is unstable and may explode or react violently.
How many of the above statements are correct?
qs.e: Only two statements are correct, 1 and 3. A waste is hazardous if it shows one or more of four traits: toxicity, ignitability, corrosivity or reactivity. A waste that is not poisonous but ignites easily or eats through containers is therefore still hazardous, and a reactive waste is an unstable one that may explode or react violently. Statement 2 fails because any single trait, toxicity included, is enough. It tempts because the four traits are always listed together. Hook: the four traits are alternatives, not joint conditions.

qs.q:
With reference to plastic in the environment, consider the following statements:
1. When a plastic bottle in the sea breaks into microplastics, it has biodegraded, that is, microbes have turned it into carbon dioxide and water.
2. Microplastics are by definition fragments of larger plastic items, so microbeads added to cleansers are not counted among them.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
qs.e: Neither statement is correct. A bottle that breaks into microplastics has only fragmented: the pieces are smaller, but the polymer is still there, because few microbes can digest it. Biodegradation would mean microbes converting it into carbon dioxide, water and biomass. Statement 2 fails because some microplastics, such as the microbeads added to cleansers and toothpaste, are manufactured small. Statement 1 tempts because the litter seems to disappear from view. Hook: plastic breaks up without breaking down; microplastics are primary when made small and secondary when formed by fragmentation.

qs.q:
Consider the following pairs of waste-treatment methods and the principle of each:
1. Sanitary landfill : A lined pit designed to stop leachate seeping into groundwater
2. Pyrolysis : Heating waste in the absence of oxygen
3. Composting : Breakdown of organic waste by microbes in the presence of oxygen Which of the pairs given above is/are correctly matched?
qs.e: All three pairs are correctly matched. A sanitary landfill is lined with clay or plastic to stop leachate, the polluted liquid seeping out of waste, from reaching soil and groundwater. Pyrolysis heats waste without oxygen, so the material breaks into char, oil and gas instead of burning. Composting is aerobic: fungi and bacteria turn organic waste into humus in the presence of oxygen. Pair 2 may be doubted by those who confuse pyrolysis with incineration, which burns waste in air. Hook: incineration uses air, pyrolysis excludes it, and composting needs it.

qs.q:
Consider the following pairs of conventions and the subject each one deals with:
1. Basel Convention : Persistent organic pollutants
2. Rotterdam Convention : Prior informed consent in the trade of certain hazardous chemicals and pesticides
3. Stockholm Convention : Movement of hazardous wastes across borders
How many of the above pairs are correctly matched?
qs.e: Only one pair, pair 2, is correctly matched. The Rotterdam Convention sets up prior informed consent, so that an importing country can agree or refuse before certain hazardous chemicals and pesticides are shipped to it. Pairs 1 and 3 exchange their subjects: the Basel Convention controls the movement of hazardous wastes across borders and their disposal, while the Stockholm Convention eliminates or restricts persistent organic pollutants. The swap tempts because these treaties all deal with toxic substances and share one secretariat. Hook: Basel covers waste on the move, Rotterdam consent before trade, Stockholm persistent pollutants, Minamata mercury.

qs.q: A plant storing a hazardous gas is damaged by an earthquake that no one could have foreseen, and the leaking gas injures people living nearby. The plant was not negligent. Under the rule of absolute liability laid down by the Supreme Court of India, which one of the following follows?
o: The plant must compensate the victims, and no defence such as an act of God is open to it.
The plant is not liable, because an act of God is a recognised defence for such an escape.
The plant is liable only if the victims can prove that it failed to take reasonable care.
The plant is not liable, because the State licensed it and must compensate the victims itself.
qs.e: Under absolute liability an enterprise engaged in a hazardous activity must compensate everyone harmed by an accident in it, whether or not it was negligent, and none of the usual defences is available. The second option describes the older rule of strict liability, which admits exceptions such as an act of God; it tempts because the earthquake was truly beyond the plant's control. Proof of carelessness is not needed, and a licence does not shift the burden to the State. Hook: strict liability has exceptions, absolute liability has none (M.C. Mehta v. Union of India, the oleum gas leak case).

qs.q:
With reference to recovering energy from city waste, consider the following statements:
1. Sorting wet waste from dry waste at source helps a waste-to-energy plant, because moisture lowers the heat value of what it burns.
2. Wet, biodegradable waste is better suited to composting or biomethanation than to burning.
3. Refuse-derived fuel is made by fermenting the wet, biodegradable part of the waste, not from its dry, combustible part.
Which one of the following conclusions, based on the above statements, is correct?
o: There are two correct statements that include statement 1.
There is only one correct statement.
qs.e: Two statements are correct, 1 and 2. A waste-to-energy plant needs dry, combustible feed; moisture lowers its calorific value, so separating wet from dry waste at source decides whether the plant works. Wet, biodegradable waste goes to composting or to biomethanation, which yields biogas. Statement 3 fails on "fermenting the wet": refuse-derived fuel is made by drying, shredding and compacting the combustible part, such as paper, plastic and wood. It tempts because fermenting wet waste does give a fuel, biogas. Hook: wet waste feeds microbes, dry waste feeds the furnace.

qs.q:
With reference to electronic waste, consider the following statements:
1. Its toxic constituents are released mainly when it is broken up, burnt or stripped with acid by crude methods, not while it is stored intact.
2. Burning cables and circuit boards in the open is a safe way to recover metal, because their plastic burns away to carbon dioxide and water.
3. It contains valuable metals such as gold and copper along with toxic ones, so it is a resource as well as a hazard.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
qs.e: Statements 1 and 3 are correct. Intact equipment keeps its lead, mercury and cadmium locked in; the danger arises when it is dismantled crudely, burnt in the open or bathed in acid. The same scrap carries gold, silver and copper, which is why it is worth recycling properly. Statement 2 fails on "safe": burning PVC and plastics treated with brominated flame retardants releases dioxins and furans, and heating solder releases lead. It tempts because burning seems a simple way to free the metal. Hook: the hazard of e-waste lies in how it is handled.

qs.q:
Consider the following statements:
Statement I: Reef-building corals under prolonged heat stress turn white.
Statement II: Heat stress makes corals expel the zooxanthellae that live in their tissue and give them most of their colour.
Statement III: Sea water that absorbs more carbon dioxide turns more acidic, which makes it harder for corals to build their skeletons.
Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements?
o: Both Statement II and Statement III are correct and both of them explain Statement I
Both Statement II and Statement III are correct, but only one of them explains Statement I
Only one of the Statements II and III is correct and that explains Statement I
Neither Statement II nor Statement III is correct
qs.e: Both reasons are correct, but only Statement II explains Statement I. Corals and their zooxanthellae live in mutualism: the algae feed the coral and colour it. Under long heat stress the partnership breaks, the algae are expelled and the white skeleton shows through, which is bleaching. Statement III is true as well, yet it does not explain Statement I: it describes a separate harm, the slowing of skeleton building as sea water turns acidic, not the heat-driven loss of algae that turns corals white. The first option tempts because both statements concern stress on reefs. Remember: heat breaks the partnership and drains the colour; acid weakens the skeleton.

qs.q:
Consider the following statements:
Statement I: Coating urea with neem oil cuts the loss of its nitrogen from the soil.
Statement II: Neem oil slows the bacterial change of ammonium into nitrate, the form of nitrogen most easily washed out of the soil.
Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements?
o: Both Statement I and Statement II are correct and Statement II explains Statement I
Both Statement I and Statement II are correct and Statement II does not explain Statement I
Statement I is correct but Statement II is not correct
Statement I is not correct but Statement II is correct
qs.e: Both statements are correct and Statement II explains Statement I. Urea breaks down in soil to ammonium, which soil particles hold; nitrifying bacteria then turn it into nitrate, which the soil does not hold, so it leaches away or is lost to the air through denitrification. Neem oil, a nitrification inhibitor, slows that step, so nitrogen stays longer in the held form. The second option tempts readers who know both facts but miss the nitrification step that joins them. Remember: neem holds nitrogen at the ammonium stage, before it becomes the nitrate that escapes.

qs.q:
Consider the following statements about mangroves:
1. Dense mangrove roots absorb wave energy, so they soften the storm surge that a cyclone drives onto a low coast.
2. By slowing the flow of water, mangroves let sediment settle, so the land around them builds up over time.
3. Mangrove soils hold carbon for long periods mainly because the daily tides keep their mud well supplied with oxygen, which protects fallen leaves and roots from decay.
4. Replanting a cleared stretch with a single fast-growing mangrove species restores the original forest once the young trees mature.
How many of the above statements are correct?
qs.e: Two statements, 1 and 2, are correct. Mangrove roots absorb wave energy and soften storm surges, and slower water lets sediment settle and build land. Statement 3 reverses the reason: their mud is short of oxygen, not rich in it, so, as in the peat of marshy soils, matter escapes decay and the blue carbon stays put. Statement 4 fails on "restores": a single-species planting cannot bring back the original mix. It tempts because replanting sounds like full repair. Remember: mangroves guard the coast, build land and bank carbon in airless mud, but a planted row is not a forest.

qs.q:
Consider the following pairs of terms used under the Ramsar Convention and their meanings:
1. Wise use : Keeping a wetland's ecological character while it is used sustainably
2. Montreux Record : A list of the best-managed Ramsar sites, held up as models for other Parties
3. Transboundary Ramsar Site : A wetland that crosses a national border, managed jointly by the countries that share it
4. Deletion of a listed site : Allowed for an urgent national interest, with compensation for the wetland lost
How many of the above pairs are correctly matched?
qs.e: Three pairs are correctly matched. Wise use means keeping a wetland's ecological character while using it sustainably; a transboundary site is one wetland across a border, managed together by the countries sharing it; and a site may be deleted for an urgent national interest, with compensation. Pair 2 fails because the Montreux Record registers sites whose ecological character has changed, is changing or is likely to change: it lists sites at risk, not model sites. It tempts because any Ramsar list sounds like an honour. Remember: Montreux is the Ramsar watch list, not its hall of fame.

qs.q:
Consider the following statements:
1. Seagrass is a flowering plant with roots, stems, leaves and vascular tissue, unlike seaweed, which has none of these.
2. A heavy load of nitrogen and phosphorus helps seagrass, because as a rooted plant it takes up the extra nutrients faster than floating algae can.
3. Eutrophication of a shallow sea can drive the dugong from an area, since it feeds on seagrass that cloudy, algae-choked water starves of light.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
qs.e: Statements 1 and 3 are correct. Seagrass is a flowering plant with roots, stems, leaves and vascular tissue, while seaweed is an alga with none of these. Statement 2 fails on its reason: surplus nitrogen and phosphorus feed algae that coat the leaves and cloud the water, so seagrass loses the light it needs. That is how eutrophication reaches the dugong, a grazer that lives on seagrass meadows. The second statement tempts because nutrients sound like plant food. Remember: in a seagrass meadow, more nutrients mean more algae and less light.

qs.q: Which one of the following best explains why the taiga is the least productive of the forest types?
o: Long, severe cold slows both growth and the decay of litter, leaving a thin, acidic, humus-poor soil
Rainfall is too scanty for the conifers, so the trees grow slowly and stand far apart on dry ground
Its conifers shed all their needles each autumn, leaving the ground bare through the winter
Permafrost lies under the whole forest, so tree roots find almost no liquid water
qs.e: The taiga is held back by cold. The long winter shortens the growing season and slows both the weathering of rock and the decay of shed needles, so its podzol is thin, acidic and poor in humus. Rainfall is not the problem: taiga conifers need little moisture. The taiga's spruce, fir and pine are evergreen, so they do not leave the ground bare each winter; permafrost keeps the tundra treeless and does not underlie the whole taiga. The rainfall option tempts because a sparse forest suggests drought. Remember: in the taiga, cold locks up the nutrients by slowing decay.

qs.q:
Consider the following observations about two tiger reserves: I. A busy new highway now separates two reserves that were once joined by a forest corridor. II. Tigers in the smaller reserve now breed only among themselves. III. Cubs with birth defects are being recorded more often in the smaller reserve. Which of the following inferences can be drawn from the above statements?
1. The highway has broken one population into isolated groups, which raises inbreeding.
2. Reconnecting the corridor, for example by raising the road on a flyover, would let genes flow between the reserves again.
3. Enlarging the inviolate core of the smaller reserve would by itself remove the risk of inbreeding.
Select the correct answer using the code given below:
qs.e: Inferences 1 and 2 can be drawn. A road that cuts a corridor traps animals in small groups, close relatives mate, and harmful recessive alleles show up more often as birth defects. Restoring the link, whether by a flyover or an underpass, lets tigers move and mix their genes again. Inference 3 fails on "by itself": a larger core gives the same small group more room but no new mates, so the gene pool stays narrow. It tempts because a bigger protected area sounds like the obvious cure. Remember: fragmentation is cured by connection, not by enlarging one fragment.

qs.q:
Consider the following statements:
1. A region qualifies as a biodiversity hotspot if it holds a very large number of endemic vascular plants, whether or not much of its natural habitat has been lost.
2. A keystone species is so called because it is the most numerous species in its community.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
qs.e: Neither statement is correct. A hotspot must pass two tests together: a very large number of endemic vascular plants, which makes it irreplaceable, and the loss of most of its original habitat, which shows it is under threat; richness alone is not enough. A keystone species is defined by influence, not numbers: its effect on the community far exceeds its abundance, as with a top predator. The second statement tempts because a common species seems to matter most. Remember: a hotspot is rich and wounded; a keystone is few in number but large in effect.

qs.q:
Consider the following pairs of conservation measures and the route of conservation each one follows:
1. Seed bank : Ex-situ conservation
2. Botanical garden : Ex-situ conservation
3. Biosphere reserve : In-situ conservation
4. Sacred grove : In-situ conservation Which of the pairs given above is/are correctly matched?
qs.e: All four pairs are correctly matched. Seed banks and botanical gardens keep plants away from their natural homes, so they are ex-situ tools. A biosphere reserve and a sacred grove both protect species where they live, the first through zoned land on the model of UNESCO's Man and the Biosphere Programme and the second through a community's faith. The third option tempts readers who feel that a grove kept by tradition is not formal conservation, but protection on site is in-situ whoever provides it. Remember: ask where the species lives; if it stays at home, the method is in-situ.

qs.q:
A community of Scheduled Tribes has lived for generations in a forest that has since become a national park and the core of a tiger reserve. Consider the following statements:
1. The community can have its forest rights recognised under the Forest Rights Act, 2006, even though the forest is now a national park, because that Act counts national parks and sanctuaries as forest land.
2. Because the Wild Life (Protection) Act, 1972 allows no rights of any person in a national park, the Forest Rights Act cannot apply anywhere inside the park.
3. Once the core is declared critical tiger habitat, no forest right can be recognised in any part of the tiger reserve, its buffer included.
Which one of the following conclusions, based on the above statements, is correct?
o: There is only one correct statement.
There are two correct statements that include statement 1.
qs.e: Only statement 1 is correct. The Forest Rights Act counts national parks and sanctuaries as forest land, so the community can claim its rights there; the Soligas won theirs inside a core. Statement 2 reads two laws as one: the wildlife law bars rights in a park, but that does not cancel the later Forest Rights Act. Statement 3 goes a step too far: the buffer is meant for co-existence, with forest rights recognised. It tempts because the wildlife law sounds absolute. Remember: two laws ask two questions; one asks who lived there, the other how the land is used.

qs.q:
With reference to the diversion of forest land for a project, consider the following statements:
1. The project must pay for compensatory afforestation, in which trees are planted on other land to make up for the forest lost.
2. It must also pay the net present value of the forest, because a new plantation cannot at once give the timber, fuelwood, carbon storage, soil protection and water recharge that the lost forest gave.
3. Even after both payments the loss is not fully made good, since a young plantation, often of one species and on scattered plots, cannot match the biodiversity of the forest it replaces.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
qs.e: All three statements are correct. A project that clears forest must fund planting elsewhere, and it also pays net present value, because a young plantation cannot at once supply the timber, fuelwood, carbon storage, soil protection and water recharge the lost forest gave. Even both payments do not make the loss neutral: plantations are often of one species and on scattered plots, so they cannot match the lost forest's biodiversity. The second option tempts readers who think money closes the account. Remember: afforestation replaces the area, net present value pays for lost services, and neither brings back the forest.

qs.q:
Consider the following statements: I. Shisham (Dalbergia sissoo) is rated Least Concern on the IUCN Red List. II. Shisham is listed in CITES Appendix II, as most of its genus is, partly because goods made from its wood are hard to tell apart from those of threatened rosewoods. III. The Schedule in which India's Wild Life (Protection) Act places a species fixes how strictly it is protected at home, and this need not follow the species' Red List category. Which of the following relationships among the above statements is/are correct?
1. Statement II is at odds with Statement I, since a species at low risk of extinction would not normally need its trade controlled.
2. Statements I and II show that the Red List and the CITES appendices answer different questions: how close a species is to extinction, and how its trade must be controlled.
3. Statement III extends to Indian law the point drawn from Statements I and II, that the strictness of protection need not match extinction risk.
Select the correct answer using the code given below:
qs.e: Relationships 2 and 3 are correct. The Red List measures how close a species is to extinction, while a CITES appendix decides how its trade across borders is controlled; shisham is Least Concern yet sits in Appendix II, partly because its wood is hard to tell from that of threatened rosewoods. India's Schedules follow their own logic too, so protection at home need not track extinction risk either. Relationship 1 fails on "at odds with": the two labels answer different questions, so a low-risk species can still need trade control. It tempts because any listing sounds like a sign of danger. Remember: the Red List asks how rare, CITES asks how traded, and the Schedule asks how protected at home.

qs.q: Which one of the following best describes the purpose of the Convention on the Conservation of Migratory Species of Wild Animals?
o: It controls international trade in wild species through a system of export and import permits
It promotes the wise use of wetlands, especially those that support large numbers of waterbirds
It provides for the fair sharing of benefits that arise from the use of genetic resources
It conserves migratory animals across their whole range through cooperation among range states
qs.e: The Convention on Migratory Species, the Bonn Convention, conserves migratory land, water and bird species across their whole range, and its Parties must strictly protect the threatened species in Appendix I. The first option describes CITES, which polices trade through permits; the second describes the Ramsar Convention, and the third the Nagoya Protocol under the CBD. The CITES option tempts because both treaties keep appendices and often list the same animals. Remember: CITES watches goods crossing borders; CMS watches the animal on its journey.

qs.q:
Consider the following observations about vultures in India: I. Carcasses of cattle treated with the painkiller diclofenac carry its residues, and vultures that feed on them die of kidney failure. II. Vulture numbers across the plains crashed, and a breeding pair raises at most one chick a year. III. Feral dogs and rats have multiplied at village carcass dumps, where carcasses now lie rotting for longer. Which of the following inferences can be drawn from the above statements?
1. The loss of vultures has handed carcasses to poorer scavengers, raising the risk that diseases such as rabies spread to people.
2. Recovery needs diclofenac kept out of livestock carcasses, and even then vulture numbers will rise only slowly, because each breeding pair adds so few young.
3. The vultures declined mainly because too few carcasses were left for them to eat.
Select the correct answer using the code given below:
qs.e: Inferences 1 and 2 can be drawn. A vulture's gut is a dead end for pathogens, so when vultures vanish, carcasses pass to dogs and rats, which carry germs onward, and open dumps breed them further. The poison sits in the carcass, so recovery needs the drug kept out of livestock, and a pair raising one chick a year means numbers climb back slowly. Inference 3 reverses the evidence: carcasses are piling up, not running short, so food shortage cannot explain the crash. It tempts because starvation is a familiar cause of decline. Remember: the vultures died of a poisoned meal, not an empty plate, and their absence feeds the dogs.

qs.q:
Consider the following statements:
1. CFCs thin the ozone layer and are also strong greenhouse gases.
2. The Kigali Amendment brought HFCs under the Montreal Protocol because they still deplete some stratospheric ozone, if far less than the CFCs they replaced.
3. Ground-level ozone in the open air is not released straight from chimneys or exhausts but forms from other pollutants, yet it is both a harmful pollutant and a greenhouse gas.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
qs.e: Statements 1 and 3 are correct. CFCs destroy stratospheric ozone and are also powerful greenhouse gases. Ground-level ozone forms in sunlight from precursors such as nitrogen oxides and volatile organic compounds rather than coming straight from a chimney or exhaust, yet it harms lungs and crops and traps heat. Statement 2 lends HFCs a trait of the HCFCs: HCFCs still harm ozone a little, but HFCs do not harm it at all, and Kigali brought them in as strong greenhouse gases. It tempts because the two families sound alike. Remember: HCFCs harm ozone a little; HFCs only warm.

qs.q:
A district in Punjab has only a few weeks between its paddy harvest and wheat sowing, and is deciding what to do with the paddy straw. Consider the following statements:
1. Burning the straw releases fine particulate matter and black carbon, but it returns all the nutrients of the straw to the soil as ash.
2. Chopping the straw and sowing wheat straight into it keeps its organic matter in the field and avoids the smoke altogether.
3. Baling the straw and sending it to a bio-CNG (compressed biogas) plant turns a crop residue into fuel away from the field.
Which one of the following conclusions, based on the above statements, is correct?
o: There is only one correct statement.
There are two correct statements that include statement 3.
qs.e: Statements 2 and 3 are correct. Sowing wheat into chopped straw is in-situ management: the residue stays in the field and makes no smoke. Baled straw sent to a bio-CNG plant is ex-situ management: the residue becomes fuel instead of smoke. Statement 1 fails on "all the nutrients": fire burns off much of what the straw holds, kills soil bacteria and fungi and dries the soil, so the ash returns only part of the nutrients. It tempts because ash looks like a fertiliser. Remember: straw left in the field feeds the soil; straw set alight feeds the smog.

qs.q: Photochemical smog is mainly a problem of hot, sunny days in traffic-heavy cities, whereas sulphurous smog is at its worst in cold, damp weather. Which one of the following best explains this difference?
o: Photochemical smog forms when strong sunlight acts on the sulphur oxides released by burning coal, while sulphurous smog builds up when nitrogen oxides from dense traffic condense on particles in cold, damp air.

Photochemical smog forms when sunlight drives reactions between nitrogen oxides and volatile organic compounds, while sulphurous smog builds up from sulphur oxides and particles trapped by a winter inversion.

Photochemical smog forms when sunlight drives reactions between nitrogen oxides and volatile organic compounds, while sulphurous smog builds up only when warm air near the ground rises and carries pollutants upward.

Both kinds of smog need strong sunlight and nitrogen oxides to form, but sulphurous smog lingers longer through the winter months because sulphur oxides break down far more slowly in cold, damp and still air.
qs.e: The second option is right. Photochemical smog is a secondary product: in strong sunlight, nitrogen oxides and volatile organic compounds react to form ozone and PAN, so it peaks on bright days. Sulphurous smog comes from sulphur oxides and particles of coal smoke; moisture from damp air condenses on them, and a winter inversion traps the mixture near the ground. The first option swaps the pollutants, the third reverses the inversion, and the fourth gives sunlight to the wrong smog. Remember: Los Angeles smog needs sun; London smog needs coal and a cold, still lid of air.

qs.q:
Consider the following statements:
Statement I: Water hyacinth spreads fastest in lakes that receive untreated sewage and farm runoff.
Statement II: Sewage and farm runoff load the water with nitrates and phosphates, and these reach open water more easily where the fringing marshes that once trapped them have been drained.
Statement III: Too many floating plants such as water hyacinth spoil a wetland's water quality, whereas the plants along its edge check erosion and help clean the water.
Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements?
o: Both Statement II and Statement III are correct and both of them explain Statement I
Both Statement II and Statement III are correct, but only one of them explains Statement I
Only one of the Statements II and III is correct and that explains Statement I
Neither Statement II nor Statement III is correct
qs.e: Both statements are correct, but only Statement II explains Statement I. Water hyacinth is a free- floating weed that multiplies when the nutrients that normally limit plant growth become plentiful; sewage and fertiliser runoff supply nitrates and phosphates, and drained marshes no longer filter them out on the way. Statement III is also true: an excess of floating plants spoils a wetland, while edge plants protect and clean it. Yet it describes what the weed does once it has spread, not why it spreads. The first option tempts because both statements deal with the lake's nutrients, plants and water quality. Remember: nutrients explain why the mat spreads; spoiled water is what it leaves behind.

qs.q:
Consider the following statements:
Statement I: A nuclear power station, though it releases no smoke, can still harm fish in the river into which it returns its cooling water.
Statement II: The returned cooling water is warmer than the river, and warm water holds less dissolved oxygen than cool water.
Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements?
o: Both Statement I and Statement II are correct and Statement II explains Statement I
Both Statement I and Statement II are correct and Statement II does not explain Statement I
Statement I is correct but Statement II is not correct
Statement I is not correct but Statement II is correct
qs.e: Both statements are correct and Statement II explains Statement I. A nuclear plant burns nothing and so gives off no smoke, but like a coal plant it uses river water for cooling and returns it several degrees warmer. That is thermal pollution: warm water holds less dissolved oxygen, and animals used to a steady temperature suffer from the sudden rise. The second option tempts readers who assume the harm must come from chemicals or radiation in the water rather than from heat itself. Remember: heat alone is a pollutant, because it drives oxygen out of water.

qs.q:
Consider the following pairs of water-quality measures and what each indicates:
1. Biochemical oxygen demand : the oxygen microbes need to break down the biodegradable organic matter in a sample
2. Chemical oxygen demand : the oxygen bacteria alone need, so it misses waste that microbes cannot digest
3. Dissolved oxygen : the oxygen actually present in the water, which falls as decaying waste uses it up
4. Turbidity : the cloudiness of water, which cuts the light reaching submerged plants and corals
How many of the above pairs are correctly matched?
qs.e: Three pairs are correctly matched. BOD measures the oxygen bacteria use to digest biodegradable waste, dissolved oxygen is what is actually left for aquatic life, and turbidity is cloudiness that blocks light. Pair 2 gives chemical oxygen demand the definition of BOD: COD counts almost all chemically oxidisable matter, including what microbes cannot digest, which is why it is the fuller gauge. The swap tempts because both measures are oxygen demands expressed per litre. Remember: B for bacteria, C for chemistry, which oxidises almost everything.

qs.q:
Consider the following statements about persistent organic pollutants (POPs):
1. They resist breakdown, so they remain in soil, water and living tissue long after their use has stopped.
2. They dissolve in fat rather than in water, so animals store them instead of excreting them, and their concentration rises at each higher trophic level.
3. They travel far on air and water currents, which is why high levels are found in Arctic marine mammals far from where the chemicals were used.
4. Some of them, such as dioxins, are never made on purpose but form as by-products when organic matter is burnt.
How many of the above statements are correct?
qs.e: All four statements are correct. POPs persist. Being fat-soluble with a long biological half-life, they are stored in fatty tissue and passed up the food chain, where each level concentrates them: biomagnification. They also move long distances on winds and currents, which explains the heavy loads in Arctic seals and whales. Dioxins are never manufactured but arise as by-products, chiefly when organic matter containing chlorine burns. Statement 3 may look doubtful to those who think POPs spread because they dissolve in water; they travel by air and currents while staying fat-soluble. Remember: persistent, fat-loving, far-travelling, food-chain-climbing.

qs.q:
With reference to waste policy, consider the following statements:
1. Extended producer responsibility applies the polluter pays principle to a product after the buyer discards it, by making the producer arrange or pay for its collection and recycling.
2. The waste hierarchy ranks recycling above reducing waste, because recycling recovers materials while reduction recovers nothing.
3. Safe disposal sits at the bottom of the waste hierarchy, even when the waste goes to a sanitary landfill lined to stop leaching.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
qs.e: Statements 1 and 3 are correct. Extended producer responsibility shifts the end-of-life cost to the producer, which is the polluter pays principle applied to products. The hierarchy runs prevent, minimise, reuse, recycle, recover and dispose, so even a lined sanitary landfill is the last resort. Statement 2 reverses the order: reduction ranks above recycling, because waste that is never made needs no energy, collection or processing. It tempts because recycling feels like the active, visible step. Remember: the best waste is the waste never made.

qs.q:
Consider the following pairs of international conventions and the main job each does:
1. Basel Convention : prior informed consent before hazardous waste is shipped across borders
2. Rotterdam Convention : elimination or restriction of persistent organic pollutants
3. Stockholm Convention : prior informed consent for international trade in listed hazardous chemicals and pesticides
4. Minamata Convention : control of mercury across its whole life cycle
How many of the above pairs are correctly matched?
qs.e: Two pairs are correctly matched. The Basel Convention controls transboundary movement of hazardous waste through notice and consent, and the Minamata Convention covers mercury from mining to emissions. Pairs 2 and 3 exchange jobs: the Rotterdam Convention runs the prior informed consent procedure for trade in certain hazardous chemicals and pesticides, while the Stockholm Convention eliminates or restricts persistent organic pollutants. The swap tempts because Rotterdam and Stockholm both deal with hazardous chemicals and hold their meetings together with Basel, and because Basel also uses prior consent. Remember: Basel moves waste, Rotterdam trades chemicals, Stockholm bans POPs, Minamata tracks mercury.

qs.q:
Consider the following observations from a canal-irrigated district: I. After two decades of heavy flooding of fields, the water table has risen close to the surface. II. A white crust appears on many fields in the dry season. III. Wheat yields have fallen, while cotton and barley still grow on the same land. Which of the following inferences can be drawn from the above statements?
1. Dry-season evaporation is drawing salty water up from the shallow water table by capillary action and leaving the salts on the surface.
2. Draining surplus water and switching to measured methods such as drip irrigation would help lower the water table and check the salt build-up.
3. Flooding the fields still more heavily, with no drainage, would wash the salts out of the soil for good.
Select the correct answer using the code given below:
qs.e: Inferences 1 and 2 can be drawn. Over-irrigation in canal tracts lifts the water table; in the dry season water creeps up through fine pores by capillary action and evaporates, leaving sodium, calcium and magnesium salts as a white crust. Salt-tolerant cotton and barley survive where wheat fails. The lasting cures are drainage that lowers the water table and careful irrigation, such as drip. Inference 3 fails on "with no drainage": salts are flushed only where water can drain away; otherwise the extra water stands, raises the table and leaves more salt behind. It tempts because leaching does need large amounts of water. Remember: salt is washed out only through a drain, never by flooding alone.

qs.q:
Consider the following pairs of soil-conservation measures and how each protects the soil:
1. Shelterbelt : slows rainwater running down a cultivated slope
2. Contour ploughing : furrows follow the steepest line of the slope and channel rainwater safely downhill
3. Groyne : a wall built parallel to the coastline that traps sand moving along the shore
How many of the above pairs are correctly matched?
qs.e: None of the pairs is correctly matched. A shelterbelt is a row of trees that slows wind on coasts and dry lands; the slope measures are contour barriers, bunds and terraces. Contour ploughing runs furrows across the slope, so ridges stop water rushing downhill; furrows running straight down the slope speed the water up and strip topsoil. A groyne does trap sand moving along the shore, but it is built at right angles to the coast, not parallel to it. Pair 3 tempts because its second half is true. Remember: trees against wind, ridges across slopes, groynes across the drift.

qs.q:
With reference to climate feedbacks, consider the following statements:
1. Warming that thaws permafrost frees methane locked in the frozen ground, and the extra methane adds to the warming: a positive feedback.
2. More frequent wildfires in a warmer world release carbon and darken the land, so they add to the warming: a positive feedback.
3. Thick, low clouds have a net warming effect on the surface, because their water droplets mainly trap outgoing heat rather than reflect sunlight.
Which one of the following conclusions, based on the above statements, is correct?
o: There are two correct statements that include statement 2.
There is only one correct statement.
qs.e: Statements 1 and 2 are correct. As permafrost thaws, long-frozen organic matter decays and trapped methane escapes, and that potent gas drives further thaw. Wildfires release carbon and darken the land, so the ground absorbs more heat and the air holds more carbon dioxide. Both loops amplify warming. Statement 3 gives low clouds the role of high ones: thick, droplet-rich low clouds reflect much sunlight and are strong coolers, while thin, high cirrus traps heat. It tempts because clouds do absorb infrared and the net cloud effect is hard to model. Remember: low and thick cools, high and thin warms.

qs.q:
With reference to the urban heat island, consider the following statements:
1. Paving over plants and water bodies means less of the sun's heat is carried away by evaporation and evapotranspiration.
2. Tall buildings let heat escape quickly to the sky, and crowded high-rise districts cool faster after sunset.
3. Light-coloured cool roofs and more trees would reduce the heat island effect, because pale surfaces reflect more sunlight and trees cool the air through evapotranspiration.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
qs.e: Statements 1 and 3 are correct. Concrete and asphalt replace the plants and water that cool a place through evaporation and evapotranspiration, and their low albedo soaks up sunlight. Raising albedo with light roofs and restoring greenery therefore cuts the excess heat. Statement 2 reverses the effect of tall buildings: they expose more surface to the sun and trap heat between them, and packed buildings keep heat islands going after dark. It tempts because height seems to bring buildings closer to open sky. Remember: dark, dry and dense makes a city hot; light, green and open cools it.

qs.q:
Consider the following statements:
1. The Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change assesses published research and does no research of its own.
2. The Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change is the forum in which countries negotiate their emission targets, while the UNFCCC only reviews the science.
3. The Shared Socioeconomic Pathways are not forecasts: each pairs a storyline about society with an emissions level, so together they map a range of possible futures rather than predict one.
How many of the above statements are correct?
qs.e: Two statements are correct. The IPCC, set up by UNEP and the WMO, has volunteer experts review published studies and does no research itself. Its scenarios pair a storyline about society with an emissions level, and they describe possible futures rather than predict one. Statement 2 swaps the bodies: countries negotiate under the UNFCCC, whose conferences produced the Kyoto Protocol and the Paris Agreement, while IPCC reports feed those talks. It tempts because both are UN bodies that work hand in hand on climate change. Remember: the IPCC reads the science; the UNFCCC bargains over it.

qs.q:
Consider the following statements about tools that put a value on emission cuts:
1. Under REDD+, developing countries are paid for the forest they plant but not for the deforestation they avoid.
2. Article 6 of the Paris Agreement allows emission cuts to be traded only through a central UN-supervised market, so countries cannot trade cuts with each other directly.
3. A green credit under India's Green Credit Programme stands for one tonne of carbon dioxide avoided and can replace a Carbon Credit Certificate towards an industry's emission-intensity target.
How many of the above statements are correct?
qs.e: No statement is correct. REDD+ exists to reward reduced emissions from deforestation and forest degradation, so avoided loss is precisely what it pays for. Statement 2 fails on "only": Article 6.2 lets two or more countries trade cuts directly; Article 6.4 is the separate central market. A green credit rewards voluntary actions such as tree planting, not only carbon cuts, and is separate from the carbon credits of the Carbon Credit Trading Scheme. Statement 3 tempts because both are tradable credits. Remember: Article 6 has two routes, and green credits are not carbon credits.

qs.q: A government wants to be certain that its country's total carbon dioxide emissions over the next decade will not exceed a fixed amount, and it is willing to let the market decide what meeting that limit costs. It is weighing a carbon tax, a cap-and-trade scheme and a target to cut emissions per unit of GDP. Which one of the following is correct?
o: A cap-and-trade scheme suits this aim, because it fixes total emissions and lets the permit price vary.
A carbon tax suits this aim, because a tax set high enough will bring emissions under the limit at a cost known in advance.
An emissions-intensity target suits this aim, because a lower intensity guarantees lower total emissions.
All three suit this aim equally, because each of them puts a fixed price on carbon.
qs.e: Cap-and-trade fits. It is a quantity instrument: the cap fixes total emissions, and trading in permits lets the market set the price. A carbon tax is the mirror image: the state fixes the price, and nobody knows in advance how high is high enough, so the total stays uncertain. Its sure cost is what makes the second option tempting. An intensity target is a ratio: if GDP grows faster than intensity falls, total emissions still rise, and it sets no price at all. Remember: tax fixes the price, cap fixes the tonnes, intensity fixes only the ratio.

qs.q:
A proposal would spray sulphate particles into the stratosphere to reflect a little sunlight, copying the cooling that follows a large volcanic eruption. Consider the following statements:
