The question cannot be answered even by using both the statements together.
qs.e:
Think it through: 1) Statement 1 alone: N = 4 is divisible by 4 but not 12; N = 12 is. Not sufficient. 2) Statement 2 alone: N = 6 fails, N = 12 works. Not sufficient. 3) Together: N is divisible by both 4 and 6, so by their LCM, 12. Sufficient. Answer (c).
Where mistakes happen: some students think 4 × 6 = 24 is needed and choose (d). Divisible by both means divisible by the LCM.

qs.q:
Question: What is the two-digit number N?

Statement 1: The sum of the digits of N is 9.
Statement 2: N is an odd multiple of 45.

The question is followed by two statements. Decide whether the data given in the statements are sufficient to answer the question.
o: The question can be answered by using one of the statements alone, but cannot be answered by using the other statement alone.
The question can be answered by using either statement alone.
The question can be answered by using both the statements together, but cannot be answered by using either statement alone.
The question cannot be answered even by using both the statements together.
qs.e:
Think it through: 1) Statement 1 alone: 18, 27, 36, 45, ... all have digit sum 9. Not sufficient. 2) Statement 2 alone: two-digit multiples of 45 are 45 and 90; the odd one is 45. N = 45. Sufficient. 3) One statement works alone and the other does not: answer (a).
Where mistakes happen: choosing (c) because the two statements 'fit together'. Always test each statement alone first; stop once you know.

qs.q: Which one of the following is a prime number?
qs.e:
Think it through: to test a number below 289 (17^2), try primes up to 13.
1) 221 = 13 × 17. 2) 247 = 13 × 19. 3) 253 = 11 × 23 (alternating sum 2 − 5 + 3 = 0, so divisible by 11). 4) 263: not divisible by 2, 3 (sum 11), 5, 7 (7 × 37 = 259, remainder 4), 11 (2 − 6 + 3 = −1), 13 (13 × 20 = 260, remainder 3). So 263 is prime.
Rule: you only need to test primes up to the square root of the number.

qs.q: How many three-digit numbers are there in which the product of the digits is 12?
qs.e:
Think it through: 1) No digit can be 0 (the product would be 0). List the sets of three digits (1 to 9) whose product is 12: {1, 2, 6}, {1, 3, 4} and {2, 2, 3}. ({1, 1, 12} fails: 12 is not a digit.) 2) Arrange each set: {1, 2, 6} gives 3! = 6 numbers; {1, 3, 4} gives 6; {2, 2, 3} has a repeated digit, so only 3 numbers (223, 232, 322). 3) Total = 6 + 6 + 3 = 15.
Where mistakes happen: missing {2, 2, 3} gives (b) 12; counting it as 6 arrangements gives (d) 18.

csat-quant-l3.title: CSAT Module Test · Quant · Number Properties · Level 3

qs.q: What is the remainder when 2^100 is divided by 13?
qs.e:
Think it through: 1) Find a power of 2 that leaves 1 on division by 13. 2^6 = 64 = 65 − 1, so 2^6 leaves −1 (that is, 12). Then 2^12 leaves (−1)² = 1. 2) 100 = 12 × 8 + 4, so 2^100 leaves the same remainder as 2^4 = 16, which is 3.
Faster: the '−1 trick' — find a power close to a multiple of the divisor, use ±1, and square if needed.
Where mistakes happen: assuming the cycle is 4 (as for unit digits) gives 2^0 → 1, option (b).

qs.q: How many factors of 10! (10 factorial) are perfect squares?
qs.e:
Think it through: 1) Prime powers in 10!: 2 → 5 + 2 + 1 = 8; 3 → 3 + 1 = 4; 5 → 2; 7 → 1. So 10! = 2^8 × 3^4 × 5^2 × 7. 2) A square factor uses even powers only: 2 → 0, 2, 4, 6, 8 (5 choices); 3 → 0, 2, 4 (3); 5 → 0, 2 (2); 7 → 0 (1). 3) Total = 5 × 3 × 2 × 1 = 30.
Where mistakes happen: miscounting the power of 2 (7 instead of 8) gives 4 × 3 × 2 = 24, option (b).

qs.q: What is the highest power of 12 that divides 40! exactly?
qs.e:
Think it through: 12 = 2² × 3. 1) Power of 2 in 40!: 20 + 10 + 5 + 2 + 1 = 38, enough for 19 twelves. 2) Power of 3: 13 + 4 + 1 = 18, enough for 18 twelves. 3) The scarcer limit wins: 12^18.
Where mistakes happen: (b) 19 counts only the 2s; the 3s run out first here — always check every prime.

qs.q: What is the sum of the digits of 10^25 − 7 ?
qs.e:
Think it through: 10^25 is 1 followed by 25 zeros. Subtracting 7 gives 24 nines followed by a 3 (try 10^3 − 7 = 993). Digit sum = 24 × 9 + 3 = 219.
Where mistakes happen: counting 25 nines (225) or 23 (210).

qs.q: What is the remainder when 1³ + 2³ + 3³ + ... + 20³ is divided by 11?
qs.e:
Think it through: 1) The sum of the first n cubes is (n(n + 1)/2)². For n = 20: (20 × 21 ÷ 2)² = 210². 2) 210 = 11 × 19 + 1, so 210 leaves 1. 3) 210² leaves 1² = 1.
Where mistakes happen: assuming 210 is divisible by 11 (it is divisible by 7, 5, 3, 2) and marking (a) 0.

qs.q: What is the smallest positive integer that has exactly 12 factors?
qs.e:
Think it through: 1) 12 factors can come from exponent patterns whose (p+1)(q+1)... = 12: 2^11; 2^5 × 3; 2^3 × 3^2; 2^2 × 3 × 5. 2) Values: 2048; 96; 72; 60. The smallest is 60. 3) Check the options: 36 = 2² × 3² has 9; 48 = 2^4 × 3 has 10; 56 = 2^3 × 7 has 8; 60 has 12.
Where mistakes happen: 72 and 96 also have 12 factors but are larger; always try spreading the exponents over the smallest primes.

qs.q: How many integers from 1 to 1000 are divisible by none of 2, 3 and 5?
qs.e:
Think it through (inclusion–exclusion): 1) Divisible by 2: 500; by 3: 333; by 5: 200. 2) By 6: 166; by 10: 100; by 15: 66. 3) By 30: 33. 4) Divisible by at least one = 500 + 333 + 200 − 166 − 100 − 66 + 33 = 734. 5) None = 1000 − 734 = 266.
Faster estimate: 1000 × (1/2) × (2/3) × (4/5) = 266.7, so 266 or 267; the exact count above settles it.
Where mistakes happen: (b) 267 rounds the estimate up; (c) 334 removes only multiples of 2 and 3 halfway.

qs.q: How many ordered pairs of positive integers (x, y) satisfy 1/x + 1/y = 1/12 ?
qs.e:
Think it through: 1) Multiply by 12xy: 12y + 12x = xy, so xy − 12x − 12y = 0. 2) Add 144 to both sides: (x − 12)(y − 12) = 144. 3) Both x and y exceed 12 (each fraction is less than 1/12), so x − 12 and y − 12 are positive divisors whose product is 144. 4) 144 = 2^4 × 3^2 has (4+1)(2+1) = 15 divisors, each giving one ordered pair.
Where mistakes happen: (a) 8 counts unordered pairs; (d) 16 adds a pair that does not exist. This is a stretch item: the algebra frame is unfamiliar, but it reduces to counting factors.

qs.q: What is the remainder when 17^23 + 23^23 is divided by 40?
qs.e:
Think it through: 1) Rule: for an odd power n, a^n + b^n is divisible by a + b. 2) Here a + b = 17 + 23 = 40 and 23 is odd. So 17^23 + 23^23 is divisible by 40. Remainder 0.
Check with small numbers: 1^3 + 3^3 = 28, divisible by 1 + 3 = 4.
Where mistakes happen: trying to find cycles for each term separately — slow and error-prone.

qs.q: How many zeros are there at the end of the product 1¹ × 2² × 3³ × 4⁴ × ... × 10¹⁰ ?
qs.e:
Think it through: 1) Count 5s; 2s are plentiful. 2) Only 5^5 and 10^10 contain 5: 5^5 gives five 5s; 10^10 = 2^10 × 5^10 gives ten. 3) Total 5s = 15, and there are far more 2s (2, 4^4, 6^6, 8^8, 10^10 ...). So 15 zeros.
Where mistakes happen: (b) 10 counts only 10^10; (a) 5 counts only 5^5.

qs.q:
Question: Is the positive integer N divisible by 15?

Statement 1: N is divisible by 5 and the sum of the digits of N is 12.
Statement 2: N² is divisible by 45.

The question is followed by two statements. Decide whether the data given in the statements are sufficient to answer the question.
o: The question can be answered by using one of the statements alone, but cannot be answered by using the other statement alone.
The question can be answered by using either statement alone.
The question can be answered by using both the statements together, but cannot be answered by using either statement alone.
The question cannot be answered even by using both the statements together.
qs.e:
Think it through: 1) Statement 1: digit sum 12 means N is divisible by 3; with 5 as well, N is divisible by 15. Sufficient. 2) Statement 2: 45 = 3² × 5. If N² has the prime 5, N must have 5; if N² has 3², N must have 3. So N is divisible by 15. Sufficient. 3) Either alone: (b).
Where mistakes happen: thinking N² divisible by 45 needs N divisible by 45 — no; a prime in N² must be in N, but only to half the power.

qs.q:
Question: What is the remainder when the positive integer N is divided by 9?

Statement 1: When N is divided by 18, the remainder is 13.
Statement 2: When N is divided by 3, the remainder is 1.

The question is followed by two statements. Decide whether the data given in the statements are sufficient to answer the question.
o: The question can be answered by using one of the statements alone, but cannot be answered by using the other statement alone.
The question can be answered by using either statement alone.
The question can be answered by using both the statements together, but cannot be answered by using either statement alone.
The question cannot be answered even by using both the statements together.
qs.e:
Think it through: 1) Statement 1: N = 18k + 13. 18k is divisible by 9, and 13 leaves 4. Remainder 4. Sufficient. 2) Statement 2: N could be 1, 4 or 7 more than a multiple of 9 (e.g. 10, 13, 16). Not sufficient. 3) Answer (a).
Where mistakes happen: treating statement 2 as enough because 'both give remainders' — a smaller divisor cannot tell you the remainder for a bigger one.

qs.q:
Consider the following statements:
1. 2^60 − 1 is divisible by 7.
2. 3^40 − 1 is divisible by 10.
3. 5^25 + 1 is divisible by 6.
4. 7^31 − 1 is divisible by 48.
How many of the above statements are correct?
qs.e:
Think it through: 1) 2^3 = 8 leaves 1 on division by 7, and 60 is a multiple of 3, so 2^60 leaves 1; 2^60 − 1 is divisible by 7. Correct. 2) 3^4 = 81 ends in 1, so 3^40 ends in 1; 3^40 − 1 ends in 0. Correct. 3) 5 leaves −1 on division by 6; (−1)^25 = −1, so 5^25 + 1 leaves 0. Correct. 4) 7^2 = 49 leaves 1 on division by 48, so 7^30 leaves 1 and 7^31 leaves 7; 7^31 − 1 leaves 6. Incorrect.
Three statements are correct.
Where mistakes happen: statement 4 looks like the others; the odd power is the trap.

qs.q: What is the sum of the digits of 123456789 × 999 ?
qs.e:
Think it through: 1) Multiply by 999 as 1000 − 1: 123456789000 − 123456789 = 123333332211. 2) Digits: 1 + 2 + 3×6 ... add carefully: 1 + 2 + 3 + 3 + 3 + 3 + 3 + 3 + 2 + 2 + 1 + 1 = 27.
Faster: any multiple of 999 is a multiple of 9, so the digit sum is a multiple of 9 — that leaves 18, 27, 36 or 45, and the subtraction settles it.
Where mistakes happen: borrowing errors in the subtraction. Check the last three digits: 000 − 789 → 211 with a borrow.

qs.q: How many three-digit numbers leave remainders 1, 2, 3 and 4 when divided by 2, 3, 4 and 5 respectively?
qs.e:
Think it through: 1) In each case the remainder is one less than the divisor, so N + 1 is divisible by 2, 3, 4 and 5 — that is, by 60. N = 60k − 1. 2) Three-digit: 100 ≤ 60k − 1 ≤ 999 → 101 ≤ 60k ≤ 1000 → k = 2 to 16. 3) That is 15 values (119, 179, ..., 959).
Where mistakes happen: starting from k = 1 (N = 59, two digits) gives 16; off-by-one when counting 2 to 16.

qs.q: What is the HCF of 2^12 − 1 and 2^18 − 1 ?
qs.e:
Think it through: 1) Rule: HCF(2^a − 1, 2^b − 1) = 2^HCF(a, b) − 1. 2) HCF(12, 18) = 6. 3) 2^6 − 1 = 63.
Check: 2^12 − 1 = 4095 = 63 × 65 and 2^18 − 1 = 262143 = 63 × 4161; 65 and 4161 share no factor.
Where mistakes happen: (d) 4095 assumes the smaller number divides the larger. This is a stretch item: the rule is rarely taught, but you can find it by factoring 2^12 − 1 = (2^6 − 1)(2^6 + 1).

qs.q: How many odd factors does 3600 have?
qs.e:
Think it through: 1) 3600 = 36 × 100 = 2^4 × 3^2 × 5^2. 2) An odd factor uses no 2. Choices: 3 → 0, 1, 2 (3); 5 → 0, 1, 2 (3). 3) Odd factors = 3 × 3 = 9.
Where mistakes happen: (d) 45 is the total number of factors (5 × 3 × 3); the 2s must be removed for odd factors.

qs.q: For how many positive integers n from 1 to 100 is n² + n + 1 divisible by 7?
qs.e:
Think it through: 1) Only n's remainder on division by 7 matters. Test r = 0 to 6: r² + r + 1 = 1, 3, 7, 13, 21, 31, 43. Divisible by 7 for r = 2 (7) and r = 4 (21). 2) n ≤ 100 with remainder 2: 2, 9, ..., 100 → 15. With remainder 4: 4, 11, ..., 95 → 14. 3) Total 29.
Where mistakes happen: 28 or 30 come from miscounting the two lists — write the first and last term of each.

qs.q: What is the remainder when 2^2026 is divided by 15?
qs.e:
Think it through: 1) 2^4 = 16 leaves 1 on division by 15. 2) 2026 = 4 × 506 + 2, so 2^2026 leaves the same as 2^2 = 4.
Where mistakes happen: using the cycle 2, 4, 8, 1 but reading remainder 2 as the 3rd term (8).

qs.q: What is the unit digit of 1¹ + 2² + 3³ + 4⁴ + ... + 10¹⁰ ?
qs.e: Think it through: unit digits — 1¹: 1; 2²: 4; 3³: 7; 4⁴: 6; 5⁵: 5; 6⁶: 6; 7⁷: 3 (cycle 7, 9, 3, 1; 7 leaves 3); 8⁸: 6 (cycle 8, 4, 2, 6); 9⁹: 9 (odd power); 10¹⁰: 0. Sum = 1 + 4 + 7 + 6 + 5 + 6 + 3 + 6 + 9 + 0 = 47 → 7.

csat-reasoning-l1.title: CSAT Module Test · Reasoning · Arrangements and Puzzles · Level 1

qs.q:
Five friends A, B, C, D and E sit in a row facing north.
• C sits in the middle of the row.
• A sits at the left end.
• B sits immediately to the right of C.
• E does not sit next to A.

Who sits at the right end of the row?
qs.e: Build it step by step. Draw five places, 1 to 5 from the left; facing north, your right is their right. A takes place 1 and C place 3. B is immediately right of C, so B is in 4. Places 2 and 5 remain for D and E. E cannot sit next to A (place 2), so E is in 5 and D in 2. Final row: A D C B E. The right end (place 5) is E.

qs.q:
Five friends A, B, C, D and E sit in a row facing north.
• C sits in the middle of the row.
• A sits at the left end.
• B sits immediately to the right of C.
• E does not sit next to A.

Who sits between A and C?
qs.e: Build it step by step. Draw five places, 1 to 5 from the left; facing north, your right is their right. A takes place 1 and C place 3. B is immediately right of C, so B is in 4. Places 2 and 5 remain for D and E. E cannot sit next to A (place 2), so E is in 5 and D in 2. Final row: A D C B E. Between A (1) and C (3) sits D (2).

qs.q:
Five friends A, B, C, D and E sit in a row facing north.
• C sits in the middle of the row.
• A sits at the left end.
• B sits immediately to the right of C.
• E does not sit next to A.

How many friends sit to the right of C?
qs.e: Build it step by step. Draw five places, 1 to 5 from the left; facing north, your right is their right. A takes place 1 and C place 3. B is immediately right of C, so B is in 4. Places 2 and 5 remain for D and E. E cannot sit next to A (place 2), so E is in 5 and D in 2. Final row: A D C B E. To the right of C (3) are B and E: two friends.

qs.q: In a class, Ravi ranks 9th from the top and 16th from the bottom. How many students are there in the class?
qs.e:
You need: total = (rank from top) + (rank from bottom) − 1, because Ravi is counted in both.
Think it through: 9 + 16 − 1 = 24.
Where mistakes happen: (c) 25 forgets to subtract Ravi, who is counted twice.

qs.q: In a row of 20 children, Meena is 7th from the left end and Asha is 5th from the right end. Meena sits to the left of Asha. How many children sit between them?
qs.e:
You need: positions from the left.
Think it through: 1) Asha is 5th from the right, so from the left she is 20 − 5 + 1 = 16th. 2) Meena is 7th. Between them: places 8 to 15, that is 15 − 8 + 1 = 8 children.
Shortcut: between = total − (left rank + right rank) = 20 − 12 = 8.

qs.q:
Among five friends P, Q, R, S and T:
• P is taller than Q.
• R is taller than P.
• S is shorter than Q.
• T is taller than R.

Who is the tallest?
qs.e: Join the clues into one chain using '>' for 'taller than': R > P > Q (first two clues), Q > S, and T > R. Chain: T > R > P > Q > S. T is the tallest.

qs.q:
Among five friends P, Q, R, S and T:
• P is taller than Q.
• R is taller than P.
• S is shorter than Q.
• T is taller than R.

Who is in the middle when the five stand in order of height?
qs.e: Join the clues into one chain using '>' for 'taller than': R > P > Q (first two clues), Q > S, and T > R. Chain: T > R > P > Q > S. The middle (3rd) of five is P.

qs.q:
Five friends A, B, C, D and E live on the five floors of a building, one on each floor. The ground floor is floor 1 and the top floor is floor 5.
• B lives on the top floor.
• D lives on the ground floor.
• C lives on the floor immediately above D.
• A does not live on floor 4.

Who lives on floor 4?
qs.e: Draw floors 5 (top) to 1. B is on 5, D on 1, C on 2. Floors 3 and 4 remain for A and E. A is not on 4, so A is on 3 and E on 4. From the bottom: D, C, A, E, B. Floor 4: E.

qs.q:
Five friends A, B, C, D and E live on the five floors of a building, one on each floor. The ground floor is floor 1 and the top floor is floor 5.
• B lives on the top floor.
• D lives on the ground floor.
• C lives on the floor immediately above D.
• A does not live on floor 4.

Who lives between C and E?
qs.e: Draw floors 5 (top) to 1. B is on 5, D on 1, C on 2. Floors 3 and 4 remain for A and E. A is not on 4, so A is on 3 and E on 4. From the bottom: D, C, A, E, B. C is on 2 and E on 4; A on 3 is between them.

qs.q:
K, L, M and N sit around a square table, one on each side, facing the centre.
• K sits opposite M.
• L sits immediately to the right of K.

Who sits immediately to the left of K?
qs.e: When people face the centre, a person's right is the next seat anticlockwise and the left is the next seat clockwise. Put K at the bottom. M is at the top (opposite). K's right is the seat anticlockwise from K, so L sits there, and N takes the last seat, on K's left. So N is immediately to K's left.

qs.q:
K, L, M and N sit around a square table, one on each side, facing the centre.
• K sits opposite M.
• L sits immediately to the right of K.

Who sits immediately to the left of L?
qs.e: When people face the centre, a person's right is the next seat anticlockwise and the left is the next seat clockwise. Put K at the bottom. M is at the top (opposite). K's right is the seat anticlockwise from K, so L sits there, and N takes the last seat, on K's left. L's left is the next seat clockwise from L, which is K's seat.

qs.q:
Five clients V, W, X, Y and Z meet a lawyer on five different days from Monday to Friday, one client a day.
• X meets her on Wednesday.
• V meets her on the day immediately after X.
• Y meets her on Monday.
• W does not meet her on Friday.

Which client meets the lawyer on Friday?
qs.e: Write Mon to Fri. Y is on Monday, X on Wednesday, V on Thursday. Tuesday and Friday remain for W and Z; W is not on Friday, so W is on Tuesday and Z on Friday. Order: Y, W, X, V, Z. Friday: Z.

qs.q:
Five clients V, W, X, Y and Z meet a lawyer on five different days from Monday to Friday, one client a day.
• X meets her on Wednesday.
• V meets her on the day immediately after X.
• Y meets her on Monday.
• W does not meet her on Friday.

How many clients meet the lawyer between Y's day and V's day?
qs.e: Write Mon to Fri. Y is on Monday, X on Wednesday, V on Thursday. Tuesday and Friday remain for W and Z; W is not on Friday, so W is on Tuesday and Z on Friday. Order: Y, W, X, V, Z. Between Monday (Y) and Thursday (V) come Tuesday (W) and Wednesday (X): two clients.

qs.q:
Among five siblings:
• Asha is older than Bela.
• Chetan is younger than Bela.
• Dev is older than Asha.
• Esha is younger than Chetan.

Who is the youngest?
qs.e: Chain with '>' meaning 'older than': Dev > Asha > Bela > Chetan > Esha. The youngest is Esha.

qs.q:
Among five siblings:
• Asha is older than Bela.
• Chetan is younger than Bela.
• Dev is older than Asha.
• Esha is younger than Chetan.

Who is the second oldest?
qs.e: Chain with '>' meaning 'older than': Dev > Asha > Bela > Chetan > Esha. Second oldest: Asha.

qs.q:
Six guests M, N, P, Q, R and S arrive at a party one after another.
• M arrives first and Q arrives last.
• S arrives just before Q.
• R arrives after M but before N.
• P arrives immediately after N.

Who arrives third?
qs.e: Places 1 to 6: M is 1, Q is 6, S is 5. Places 2, 3 and 4 remain for R, N and P. R comes before N, and P comes right after N, so R is 2, N is 3 and P is 4. Order: M, R, N, P, S, Q. Third: N.

qs.q:
Six guests M, N, P, Q, R and S arrive at a party one after another.
• M arrives first and Q arrives last.
• S arrives just before Q.
• R arrives after M but before N.
• P arrives immediately after N.

How many guests arrive between R and S?
qs.e: Places 1 to 6: M is 1, Q is 6, S is 5. Places 2, 3 and 4 remain for R, N and P. R comes before N, and P comes right after N, so R is 2, N is 3 and P is 4. Order: M, R, N, P, S, Q. Between R (2) and S (5) arrive N and P: two guests.

qs.q: In how many different ways can three people sit in a row of three chairs?
qs.e:
You need: count choices place by place.
Think it through: the first chair can take any of 3 people, the second any of the remaining 2, the third the last 1. 3 × 2 × 1 = 6.
List them to check: ABC, ACB, BAC, BCA, CAB, CBA.

qs.q: In how many different ways can four people sit around a round table? (Two seatings are the same if everyone has the same neighbours on the same sides.)
qs.e:
You need: around a circle, turning everyone one seat round does not make a new seating.
Think it through: fix one person's seat. The other 3 can be arranged in 3 × 2 × 1 = 6 ways.
Rule: n people around a round table → (n − 1)! ways.
Where mistakes happen: (d) 24 treats the circle like a row.

qs.q: In a row of 30 students, Kiran is 12th from the left end. What is Kiran's position from the right end?
qs.e:
You need: position from right = total − position from left + 1.
Think it through: 30 − 12 + 1 = 19.
Check: 11 students on his left, 18 on his right; 11 + 1 + 18 = 30.

csat-reasoning-l2.title: CSAT Module Test · Reasoning · Arrangements and Puzzles · Level 2

qs.q:
Six friends P, Q, R, S, T and U sit in a row facing north.
• R sits at one of the ends of the row.
• Exactly two people sit between R and T.
• Q sits immediately to the right of T.
• U does not sit next to Q.
• P sits somewhere to the left of S.
• S does not sit at the right end.

Who sits third from the left end?
qs.e: Places 1 to 6 from the left; facing north, their right is your right. 1) R is at an end with two people between R and T. If R is at 1, T is at 4 and Q at 5; then the right end (6) must go to P, U or S — S cannot (clue 6), U cannot (next to Q), and P cannot (P is left of S). So R is NOT at 1. 2) R is at 6, T at 3, Q at 4. 3) Places 1, 2 and 5 remain for P, S and U. U cannot be at 5 (next to Q), so S is at 5 (P must be left of S, so S takes the right-most free place). P and U fill 1 and 2 in either order. Two arrangements: P U T Q S R or U P T Q S R. In both, T is third from the left.

qs.q:
Six friends P, Q, R, S, T and U sit in a row facing north.
• R sits at one of the ends of the row.
• Exactly two people sit between R and T.
• Q sits immediately to the right of T.
• U does not sit next to Q.
• P sits somewhere to the left of S.
• S does not sit at the right end.

Which one of the following is definitely true?
o: S sits second from the right end.
P sits at the left end.
Exactly one person sits between P and T.
qs.e: Places 1 to 6 from the left; facing north, their right is your right. 1) R is at an end with two people between R and T. If R is at 1, T is at 4 and Q at 5; then the right end (6) must go to P, U or S — S cannot (clue 6), U cannot (next to Q), and P cannot (P is left of S). So R is NOT at 1. 2) R is at 6, T at 3, Q at 4. 3) Places 1, 2 and 5 remain for P, S and U. U cannot be at 5 (next to Q), so S is at 5 (P must be left of S, so S takes the right-most free place). P and U fill 1 and 2 in either order. Two arrangements: P U T Q S R or U P T Q S R. S is at place 5 (second from the right) in both. (b) and (c) hold in only one arrangement each; (d) is true only when P is at 1.

qs.q:
Six friends P, Q, R, S, T and U sit in a row facing north.
• R sits at one of the ends of the row.
• Exactly two people sit between R and T.
• Q sits immediately to the right of T.
• U does not sit next to Q.
• P sits somewhere to the left of S.
• S does not sit at the right end.

If U sits at an end of the row, who sits second from the left end?
qs.e: Places 1 to 6 from the left; facing north, their right is your right. 1) R is at an end with two people between R and T. If R is at 1, T is at 4 and Q at 5; then the right end (6) must go to P, U or S — S cannot (clue 6), U cannot (next to Q), and P cannot (P is left of S). So R is NOT at 1. 2) R is at 6, T at 3, Q at 4. 3) Places 1, 2 and 5 remain for P, S and U. U cannot be at 5 (next to Q), so S is at 5 (P must be left of S, so S takes the right-most free place). P and U fill 1 and 2 in either order. Two arrangements: P U T Q S R or U P T Q S R. If U is at an end, U is at 1, so P is at 2.

qs.q:
Six people A, B, C, D, E and F sit around a circular table, equally spaced, facing the centre.
• B sits opposite A.
• C sits immediately to the right of A.
• D does not sit next to B.
• E sits next to C.

Who sits opposite D?
qs.e: Facing the centre: right = next seat anticlockwise, left = next seat clockwise. Number seats 0 to 5 clockwise with A at 0. B is opposite, at 3. C is A's right, at 5. E is next to C: seat 4 (seat 0 is A). Seats 1 and 2 remain for D and F; D cannot be next to B (seat 2), so D is at 1 and F at 2. Clockwise from A: A, D, F, B, E, C. D is at 1; the seat opposite is 4, where E sits.

qs.q:
Six people A, B, C, D, E and F sit around a circular table, equally spaced, facing the centre.
• B sits opposite A.
• C sits immediately to the right of A.
• D does not sit next to B.
• E sits next to C.

Who sits immediately to the right of F?
qs.e: Facing the centre: right = next seat anticlockwise, left = next seat clockwise. Number seats 0 to 5 clockwise with A at 0. B is opposite, at 3. C is A's right, at 5. E is next to C: seat 4 (seat 0 is A). Seats 1 and 2 remain for D and F; D cannot be next to B (seat 2), so D is at 1 and F at 2. Clockwise from A: A, D, F, B, E, C. F is at 2; F's right is anticlockwise, seat 1: D.

qs.q:
Six people A, B, C, D, E and F sit around a circular table, equally spaced, facing the centre.
• B sits opposite A.
• C sits immediately to the right of A.
• D does not sit next to B.
• E sits next to C.

Counting clockwise from A, how many people sit between A and F?
qs.e: Facing the centre: right = next seat anticlockwise, left = next seat clockwise. Number seats 0 to 5 clockwise with A at 0. B is opposite, at 3. C is A's right, at 5. E is next to C: seat 4 (seat 0 is A). Seats 1 and 2 remain for D and F; D cannot be next to B (seat 2), so D is at 1 and F at 2. Clockwise from A: A, D, F, B, E, C. Clockwise from A (0): D (1), then F (2). One person between.

qs.q:
Six people J, K, L, M, N and O live on the six floors of a building, one on each floor (floor 1 is the lowest, floor 6 the top). Each is from a different city: Agra, Bhopal, Chennai, Delhi, Indore and Pune.
• L lives on floor 3 and is from Pune.
• J lives on an even-numbered floor above L and is from Indore.
• The person from Delhi lives on the floor immediately above J.
• K lives on floor 1.
• O lives on the floor immediately above M.
• O is from Chennai.
• N is from either Delhi or Agra.

Who lives on the top floor?
qs.e: 1) J is above floor 3 on an even floor: 4 or 6. Someone lives immediately above J, so J is not on 6: J is on 4, and the Delhi person is on 5. 2) K is on 1. Floors 2, 5 and 6 remain for M, N and O. O is immediately above M, so M–O is 5–6 (2 has nothing directly above it free). N is on 2. 3) The Delhi person is on 5 = M. N is then from Agra. O is from Chennai, J Indore, L Pune, so K is from Bhopal. Floors 1 to 6: K (Bhopal), N (Agra), L (Pune), J (Indore), M (Delhi), O (Chennai). Top floor: O.

qs.q:
Six people J, K, L, M, N and O live on the six floors of a building, one on each floor (floor 1 is the lowest, floor 6 the top). Each is from a different city: Agra, Bhopal, Chennai, Delhi, Indore and Pune.
• L lives on floor 3 and is from Pune.
• J lives on an even-numbered floor above L and is from Indore.
• The person from Delhi lives on the floor immediately above J.
• K lives on floor 1.
• O lives on the floor immediately above M.
• O is from Chennai.
• N is from either Delhi or Agra.

The person living on floor 2 is from which city?
qs.e: 1) J is above floor 3 on an even floor: 4 or 6. Someone lives immediately above J, so J is not on 6: J is on 4, and the Delhi person is on 5. 2) K is on 1. Floors 2, 5 and 6 remain for M, N and O. O is immediately above M, so M–O is 5–6 (2 has nothing directly above it free). N is on 2. 3) The Delhi person is on 5 = M. N is then from Agra. O is from Chennai, J Indore, L Pune, so K is from Bhopal. Floors 1 to 6: K (Bhopal), N (Agra), L (Pune), J (Indore), M (Delhi), O (Chennai). Floor 2: N, from Agra.

qs.q:
Six people J, K, L, M, N and O live on the six floors of a building, one on each floor (floor 1 is the lowest, floor 6 the top). Each is from a different city: Agra, Bhopal, Chennai, Delhi, Indore and Pune.
• L lives on floor 3 and is from Pune.
• J lives on an even-numbered floor above L and is from Indore.
• The person from Delhi lives on the floor immediately above J.
• K lives on floor 1.
• O lives on the floor immediately above M.
• O is from Chennai.
• N is from either Delhi or Agra.

How many people live between K and the person from Delhi?
qs.e: 1) J is above floor 3 on an even floor: 4 or 6. Someone lives immediately above J, so J is not on 6: J is on 4, and the Delhi person is on 5. 2) K is on 1. Floors 2, 5 and 6 remain for M, N and O. O is immediately above M, so M–O is 5–6 (2 has nothing directly above it free). N is on 2. 3) The Delhi person is on 5 = M. N is then from Agra. O is from Chennai, J Indore, L Pune, so K is from Bhopal. Floors 1 to 6: K (Bhopal), N (Agra), L (Pune), J (Indore), M (Delhi), O (Chennai). K is on 1, the Delhi person (M) on 5: floors 2, 3 and 4 lie between — three people.

qs.q:
Six lectures — Economics, Geography, History, Maths, Polity and Science — are held on six days from Monday to Saturday, one lecture a day.
• Polity is on Wednesday.
• Science is on the day immediately before Geography.
• History is held after Maths, but not on the day immediately after it.
• Economics is neither on the first day nor on the last day.
• Maths is not on Monday.

Which lecture is held on Saturday?
qs.e: Write Mon to Sat with Polity on Wed. Science–Geography is a back-to-back pair, so it takes Mon–Tue, Thu–Fri or Fri–Sat. Test each. Thu–Fri: Mon, Tue and Sat are left for Economics, Maths and History. Economics cannot be Mon or Sat, so it is Tue; Maths cannot be Mon, so Maths is Sat — and History cannot come after it. Fails. Fri–Sat: Mon, Tue and Thu are left. Maths is Tue or Thu. If Maths is Tue, History must be Thu, leaving Economics on Mon — not allowed. If Maths is Thu, no day is left two days later. Fails. Mon–Tue: Thu, Fri and Sat are left. History must be at least two days after Maths: Maths Thu, History Sat, Economics Fri. Works. Order: Science, Geography, Polity, Maths, Economics, History. Saturday: History.

qs.q:
Six lectures — Economics, Geography, History, Maths, Polity and Science — are held on six days from Monday to Saturday, one lecture a day.
• Polity is on Wednesday.
• Science is on the day immediately before Geography.
• History is held after Maths, but not on the day immediately after it.
• Economics is neither on the first day nor on the last day.
• Maths is not on Monday.

On which day is the Maths lecture held?
qs.e: Write Mon to Sat with Polity on Wed. Science–Geography is a back-to-back pair, so it takes Mon–Tue, Thu–Fri or Fri–Sat. Test each. Thu–Fri: Mon, Tue and Sat are left for Economics, Maths and History. Economics cannot be Mon or Sat, so it is Tue; Maths cannot be Mon, so Maths is Sat — and History cannot come after it. Fails. Fri–Sat: Mon, Tue and Thu are left. Maths is Tue or Thu. If Maths is Tue, History must be Thu, leaving Economics on Mon — not allowed. If Maths is Thu, no day is left two days later. Fails. Mon–Tue: Thu, Fri and Sat are left. History must be at least two days after Maths: Maths Thu, History Sat, Economics Fri. Works. Order: Science, Geography, Polity, Maths, Economics, History. Maths is on Thursday.

qs.q:
Six lectures — Economics, Geography, History, Maths, Polity and Science — are held on six days from Monday to Saturday, one lecture a day.
• Polity is on Wednesday.
• Science is on the day immediately before Geography.
• History is held after Maths, but not on the day immediately after it.
• Economics is neither on the first day nor on the last day.
• Maths is not on Monday.

How many lectures are held between Science and Economics?
qs.e: Write Mon to Sat with Polity on Wed. Science–Geography is a back-to-back pair, so it takes Mon–Tue, Thu–Fri or Fri–Sat. Test each. Thu–Fri: Mon, Tue and Sat are left for Economics, Maths and History. Economics cannot be Mon or Sat, so it is Tue; Maths cannot be Mon, so Maths is Sat — and History cannot come after it. Fails. Fri–Sat: Mon, Tue and Thu are left. Maths is Tue or Thu. If Maths is Tue, History must be Thu, leaving Economics on Mon — not allowed. If Maths is Thu, no day is left two days later. Fails. Mon–Tue: Thu, Fri and Sat are left. History must be at least two days after Maths: Maths Thu, History Sat, Economics Fri. Works. Order: Science, Geography, Polity, Maths, Economics, History. Science (Mon) and Economics (Fri): Tue, Wed and Thu lie between — three lectures.

qs.q:
Six students A, B, C, D, E and F are compared by height.
• A is taller than B but shorter than C.
• D is shorter than B.
• E is taller than C.
• F is shorter than A but taller than B.

Who is the third tallest?
qs.e: Chain with '>' for taller: C > A > B, E > C, A > F > B, B > D. Joined: E > C > A > F > B > D. Third tallest: A.

qs.q:
Six students A, B, C, D, E and F are compared by height.
• A is taller than B but shorter than C.
• D is shorter than B.
• E is taller than C.
• F is shorter than A but taller than B.

A seventh student G joins. G is taller than F but shorter than C. Which one of the following is definitely true?
o: Exactly two students are taller than G.
G is the third tallest of the seven.
qs.e: Chain with '>' for taller: C > A > B, E > C, A > F > B, B > D. Joined: E > C > A > F > B > D. G lies somewhere between C and F, but we do not know whether G is above or below A. So (a), (c) and (b) may or may not hold. G is below C, and C is below E, so G is definitely shorter than E.

qs.q: In a row of students, Kavya is 14th from the left end and Rohan is 17th from the right end. When they exchange places, Kavya becomes 22nd from the left end. How many students are in the row?
qs.e:
Think it through: 1) After the exchange, Kavya stands where Rohan stood. So Rohan's place is 22nd from the left. 2) Rohan's place is also 17th from the right. 3) Total = 22 + 17 − 1 = 38.
Where mistakes happen: using Kavya's old rank 14 with 17 gives 30 (not offered); forgetting the −1 gives 39.

qs.q: In a queue, Amit is 10th from the front and Bina is 25th from the back. There are exactly 8 people between Amit and Bina. What is the largest possible number of people in the queue?
qs.e:
Think it through: two cases.
Case 1 — Amit ahead of Bina: Amit 10th, 8 between, so Bina is 19th from the front. Total = 19 + 25 − 1 = 43.
Case 2 — Bina ahead of Amit: Bina is 10 − 9 = 1st from the front. Then she is also 25th from the back, so the queue has 25 people.
Largest possible: 43.
Where mistakes happen: considering only one case; (d) 44 forgets the −1.

qs.q:
Eight people P, Q, R, S, T, U, V and W sit around a circular table, equally spaced, facing the centre.
• T sits opposite P.
• Q sits second to the right of P.
• R sits immediately to the left of T.
• S sits opposite Q.
• U is an immediate neighbour of P.
• V does not sit immediately to the left of S.

Who sits immediately to the right of T?
qs.e: Facing the centre: right = anticlockwise, left = clockwise. Seats 0–7 clockwise, P at 0. T opposite: 4. Q is second to P's right: seat 6. R is T's left (clockwise): 5. S is opposite Q: 2. Seats 1, 3 and 7 remain for U, V and W. U is next to P: seat 1 or 7. V cannot be at S's left (seat 3), so W is at 3. U and V take 1 and 7 in either order — two arrangements. T is at 4; T's right is seat 3: W in both arrangements.

qs.q:
Eight people P, Q, R, S, T, U, V and W sit around a circular table, equally spaced, facing the centre.
• T sits opposite P.
• Q sits second to the right of P.
• R sits immediately to the left of T.
• S sits opposite Q.
• U is an immediate neighbour of P.
• V does not sit immediately to the left of S.

Which one of the following is definitely true?
o: S sits immediately to the left of P.
qs.e: Facing the centre: right = anticlockwise, left = clockwise. Seats 0–7 clockwise, P at 0. T opposite: 4. Q is second to P's right: seat 6. R is T's left (clockwise): 5. S is opposite Q: 2. Seats 1, 3 and 7 remain for U, V and W. U is next to P: seat 1 or 7. V cannot be at S's left (seat 3), so W is at 3. U and V take 1 and 7 in either order — two arrangements. U is at 1 or 7, next to P either way. V sits opposite R only if V is at 1. W (3) is not next to Q (6). P's left is seat 1, not S's seat 2.

qs.q: In how many ways can five different books be arranged in a row on a shelf if two particular books must always be kept together?
qs.e:
Think it through: 1) Tie the two books together into one bundle. Now there are 4 items to arrange: 4 × 3 × 2 × 1 = 24 ways. 2) Inside the bundle, the two books can be in 2 orders. 3) Total = 24 × 2 = 48.
Where mistakes happen: (a) 24 forgets the order inside the bundle.

qs.q: In how many ways can five people A, B, C, D and E sit in a row if A and B must NOT sit next to each other?
qs.e:
Think it through: 1) All arrangements: 5! = 120. 2) Arrangements with A and B together: 4! × 2 = 48 (as in a bundle). 3) Not together = 120 − 48 = 72.
Where mistakes happen: (a) 48 gives the 'together' count instead.

csat-reasoning-l3.title: CSAT Module Test · Reasoning · Arrangements and Puzzles · Level 3

qs.q:
Eight people A, B, C, D, E, F, G and H sit around a circular table, equally spaced. Exactly four of them face the centre and the other four face away from the centre.
• A faces the centre. B sits third to the right of A.
• C sits opposite B and faces away from the centre.
• D sits immediately to the right of C.
• E sits second to the left of D, and E faces the same direction as D.
• F sits immediately to the right of A, and F does not face the same direction as A.
• G sits immediately to the right of B and faces the centre.

Who sits immediately to the left of H?
qs.e: Rules: a person facing the centre has right = anticlockwise, left = clockwise; a person facing away has right = clockwise, left = anticlockwise. Seats 0–7 clockwise, A at 0 facing in. 1) B is third to A's right (anticlockwise): seat 5. 2) C opposite B: seat 1, facing out. 3) D is C's right; C faces out, so right is clockwise: seat 2. 4) F is A's right: seat 7, facing out. 5) E is second to D's left and faces like D: if D faced out, D's left would be anticlockwise and seat 0 is A — impossible; so D faces in, its left is clockwise and E is at 4, facing in. 6) G is B's right and faces in. Seats left: 3 and 6. If B faced in, its right (anticlockwise) is 4 — taken by E; so B faces out and its right is clockwise, seat 6: G. 7) H takes seat 3. Facing count: in = A, D, E, G (four), so H faces out. Clockwise: A(in), C(out), D(in), H(out), E(in), B(out), G(in), F(out). H faces out, so H's left is anticlockwise: seat 2, D.

qs.q:
Eight people A, B, C, D, E, F, G and H sit around a circular table, equally spaced. Exactly four of them face the centre and the other four face away from the centre.
• A faces the centre. B sits third to the right of A.
• C sits opposite B and faces away from the centre.
• D sits immediately to the right of C.
• E sits second to the left of D, and E faces the same direction as D.
• F sits immediately to the right of A, and F does not face the same direction as A.
• G sits immediately to the right of B and faces the centre.

Which one of the following pairs consists of two people who both face away from the centre?
qs.e: Rules: a person facing the centre has right = anticlockwise, left = clockwise; a person facing away has right = clockwise, left = anticlockwise. Seats 0–7 clockwise, A at 0 facing in. 1) B is third to A's right (anticlockwise): seat 5. 2) C opposite B: seat 1, facing out. 3) D is C's right; C faces out, so right is clockwise: seat 2. 4) F is A's right: seat 7, facing out. 5) E is second to D's left and faces like D: if D faced out, D's left would be anticlockwise and seat 0 is A — impossible; so D faces in, its left is clockwise and E is at 4, facing in. 6) G is B's right and faces in. Seats left: 3 and 6. If B faced in, its right (anticlockwise) is 4 — taken by E; so B faces out and its right is clockwise, seat 6: G. 7) H takes seat 3. Facing count: in = A, D, E, G (four), so H faces out. Clockwise: A(in), C(out), D(in), H(out), E(in), B(out), G(in), F(out). Facing away: C, H, B and F. Only the pair C and H are both facing away.

qs.q:
Eight people A, B, C, D, E, F, G and H sit around a circular table, equally spaced. Exactly four of them face the centre and the other four face away from the centre.
• A faces the centre. B sits third to the right of A.
• C sits opposite B and faces away from the centre.
• D sits immediately to the right of C.
• E sits second to the left of D, and E faces the same direction as D.
• F sits immediately to the right of A, and F does not face the same direction as A.
• G sits immediately to the right of B and faces the centre.

Who sits third to the right of C?
qs.e: Rules: a person facing the centre has right = anticlockwise, left = clockwise; a person facing away has right = clockwise, left = anticlockwise. Seats 0–7 clockwise, A at 0 facing in. 1) B is third to A's right (anticlockwise): seat 5. 2) C opposite B: seat 1, facing out. 3) D is C's right; C faces out, so right is clockwise: seat 2. 4) F is A's right: seat 7, facing out. 5) E is second to D's left and faces like D: if D faced out, D's left would be anticlockwise and seat 0 is A — impossible; so D faces in, its left is clockwise and E is at 4, facing in. 6) G is B's right and faces in. Seats left: 3 and 6. If B faced in, its right (anticlockwise) is 4 — taken by E; so B faces out and its right is clockwise, seat 6: G. 7) H takes seat 3. Facing count: in = A, D, E, G (four), so H faces out. Clockwise: A(in), C(out), D(in), H(out), E(in), B(out), G(in), F(out). C faces away, so C's right is clockwise: seats 2, 3, 4 — third is seat 4, E.

qs.q:
Seven people A, B, C, D, E, F and G live on the seven floors of a building, one on each floor (floor 1 is the lowest, floor 7 the top).
• B lives below E, and exactly two people live between them.
• C lives on an odd-numbered floor above E.
• A lives on the floor immediately above F, and F lives on an even-numbered floor.
• At least two people live between C and D.
• G lives neither on the lowest floor nor on the top floor.
• G does not live on a floor next to E's floor.

Who lives on the floor immediately below E?
qs.e: Work by cases on E, because B is exactly three floors below E (two people between) and C is on an odd floor above E. E can be 4, 5 or 6 (B needs a floor 3 below). Case E = 6: B = 3, C = 7. F is even with A just above: F = 2 gives A = 3 (taken by B), so F = 4, A = 5. Floors 1 and 2 remain for D and G; G is not on floor 1, so G = 2, D = 1. Check: G (2) is not next to E (6); C (7) and D (1) have five people between them. Works. Case E = 5: B = 2, C = 7. F even, A above: F = 4 (A 5 taken by E) fails; F = 6 gives A = 7 (taken). No room. Case E = 4: B = 1, C = 5 or 7; F = 2 gives A = 3, F = 6 gives A = 7; testing the remaining clues (G not on 1 or 7, not next to E; D at least three floors from C) leaves no arrangement. Answer from the bottom: D, G, B, F, A, E, C. E is on 6; floor 5 is A.

qs.q:
Seven people A, B, C, D, E, F and G live on the seven floors of a building, one on each floor (floor 1 is the lowest, floor 7 the top).
• B lives below E, and exactly two people live between them.
• C lives on an odd-numbered floor above E.
• A lives on the floor immediately above F, and F lives on an even-numbered floor.
• At least two people live between C and D.
• G lives neither on the lowest floor nor on the top floor.
• G does not live on a floor next to E's floor.

How many people live between G and C?
qs.e: Work by cases on E, because B is exactly three floors below E (two people between) and C is on an odd floor above E. E can be 4, 5 or 6 (B needs a floor 3 below). Case E = 6: B = 3, C = 7. F is even with A just above: F = 2 gives A = 3 (taken by B), so F = 4, A = 5. Floors 1 and 2 remain for D and G; G is not on floor 1, so G = 2, D = 1. Check: G (2) is not next to E (6); C (7) and D (1) have five people between them. Works. Case E = 5: B = 2, C = 7. F even, A above: F = 4 (A 5 taken by E) fails; F = 6 gives A = 7 (taken). No room. Case E = 4: B = 1, C = 5 or 7; F = 2 gives A = 3, F = 6 gives A = 7; testing the remaining clues (G not on 1 or 7, not next to E; D at least three floors from C) leaves no arrangement. Answer from the bottom: D, G, B, F, A, E, C. G is on 2, C on 7: floors 3, 4, 5 and 6 lie between — four people.

qs.q:
Seven people A, B, C, D, E, F and G live on the seven floors of a building, one on each floor (floor 1 is the lowest, floor 7 the top).
• B lives below E, and exactly two people live between them.
• C lives on an odd-numbered floor above E.
• A lives on the floor immediately above F, and F lives on an even-numbered floor.
• At least two people live between C and D.
• G lives neither on the lowest floor nor on the top floor.
• G does not live on a floor next to E's floor.

If D and A exchange floors, who will live immediately above D?
qs.e: Work by cases on E, because B is exactly three floors below E (two people between) and C is on an odd floor above E. E can be 4, 5 or 6 (B needs a floor 3 below). Case E = 6: B = 3, C = 7. F is even with A just above: F = 2 gives A = 3 (taken by B), so F = 4, A = 5. Floors 1 and 2 remain for D and G; G is not on floor 1, so G = 2, D = 1. Check: G (2) is not next to E (6); C (7) and D (1) have five people between them. Works. Case E = 5: B = 2, C = 7. F even, A above: F = 4 (A 5 taken by E) fails; F = 6 gives A = 7 (taken). No room. Case E = 4: B = 1, C = 5 or 7; F = 2 gives A = 3, F = 6 gives A = 7; testing the remaining clues (G not on 1 or 7, not next to E; D at least three floors from C) leaves no arrangement. Answer from the bottom: D, G, B, F, A, E, C. After the exchange D is on 5, and floor 6 above is E.

qs.q:
Eight people sit in two parallel rows of four seats each, the rows facing each other. P, Q, R and S sit in Row 1 and face south. W, X, Y and Z sit in Row 2 and face north. Each person in one row faces exactly one person in the other row. Seats in both rows are numbered 1 to 4 from west to east.
• Q sits at one end of Row 1 and faces Y.
• X sits second to the right of Y.
• R sits immediately to the left of Q.
• W does not face R.
• S sits at one end of Row 1.

Who faces P?
qs.e: Directions: Row 1 faces south, so a Row 1 person's right is west and left is east. Row 2 faces north, so right is east. 1) X is second to Y's right (east): Y is in seat 1 or 2. Q faces Y, so Q is in the same seat number; Q is at an end, so Q and Y are in seat 1, and X is in seat 3. 2) R is immediately to Q's left (east): seat 2. 3) S is at an end of Row 1: seat 4; P takes seat 3. 4) W and Z fill Row 2 seats 2 and 4. W does not face R (seat 2), so W is in 4 and Z in 2. Row 1 (west to east): Q, R, P, S. Row 2: Y, Z, X, W. Facing pairs: Q–Y, R–Z, P–X, S–W. P (seat 3) faces X.

qs.q:
Eight people sit in two parallel rows of four seats each, the rows facing each other. P, Q, R and S sit in Row 1 and face south. W, X, Y and Z sit in Row 2 and face north. Each person in one row faces exactly one person in the other row. Seats in both rows are numbered 1 to 4 from west to east.
• Q sits at one end of Row 1 and faces Y.
• X sits second to the right of Y.
• R sits immediately to the left of Q.
• W does not face R.
• S sits at one end of Row 1.

Who sits immediately to the right of P?
qs.e: Directions: Row 1 faces south, so a Row 1 person's right is west and left is east. Row 2 faces north, so right is east. 1) X is second to Y's right (east): Y is in seat 1 or 2. Q faces Y, so Q is in the same seat number; Q is at an end, so Q and Y are in seat 1, and X is in seat 3. 2) R is immediately to Q's left (east): seat 2. 3) S is at an end of Row 1: seat 4; P takes seat 3. 4) W and Z fill Row 2 seats 2 and 4. W does not face R (seat 2), so W is in 4 and Z in 2. Row 1 (west to east): Q, R, P, S. Row 2: Y, Z, X, W. Facing pairs: Q–Y, R–Z, P–X, S–W. P faces south, so P's right is west: seat 2, R.

qs.q:
Eight people sit in two parallel rows of four seats each, the rows facing each other. P, Q, R and S sit in Row 1 and face south. W, X, Y and Z sit in Row 2 and face north. Each person in one row faces exactly one person in the other row. Seats in both rows are numbered 1 to 4 from west to east.
• Q sits at one end of Row 1 and faces Y.
• X sits second to the right of Y.
• R sits immediately to the left of Q.
• W does not face R.
• S sits at one end of Row 1.

Who sit at the two ends of Row 2?
qs.e: Directions: Row 1 faces south, so a Row 1 person's right is west and left is east. Row 2 faces north, so right is east. 1) X is second to Y's right (east): Y is in seat 1 or 2. Q faces Y, so Q is in the same seat number; Q is at an end, so Q and Y are in seat 1, and X is in seat 3. 2) R is immediately to Q's left (east): seat 2. 3) S is at an end of Row 1: seat 4; P takes seat 3. 4) W and Z fill Row 2 seats 2 and 4. W does not face R (seat 2), so W is in 4 and Z in 2. Row 1 (west to east): Q, R, P, S. Row 2: Y, Z, X, W. Facing pairs: Q–Y, R–Z, P–X, S–W. Row 2 ends: Y (seat 1) and W (seat 4).

qs.q:
Eight people sit in two parallel rows of four seats each, the rows facing each other. P, Q, R and S sit in Row 1 and face south. W, X, Y and Z sit in Row 2 and face north. Each person in one row faces exactly one person in the other row. Seats in both rows are numbered 1 to 4 from west to east.
• Q sits at one end of Row 1 and faces Y.
• X sits second to the right of Y.
• R sits immediately to the left of Q.
• W does not face R.
• S sits at one end of Row 1.

Who faces S?
qs.e: Directions: Row 1 faces south, so a Row 1 person's right is west and left is east. Row 2 faces north, so right is east. 1) X is second to Y's right (east): Y is in seat 1 or 2. Q faces Y, so Q is in the same seat number; Q is at an end, so Q and Y are in seat 1, and X is in seat 3. 2) R is immediately to Q's left (east): seat 2. 3) S is at an end of Row 1: seat 4; P takes seat 3. 4) W and Z fill Row 2 seats 2 and 4. W does not face R (seat 2), so W is in 4 and Z in 2. Row 1 (west to east): Q, R, P, S. Row 2: Y, Z, X, W. Facing pairs: Q–Y, R–Z, P–X, S–W. S (seat 4) faces W.

qs.q:
Five teachers A, B, C, D and E each teach one class on a different day from Monday to Friday, and each teaches a different subject: Art, Biology, Chemistry, Drama or English.
• C teaches on Wednesday.
• The Biology class is on the day immediately after the Art class.
• B teaches Drama, but not on Monday or Friday.
• The English class is on Friday, and E does not teach English.
• A teaches on the day immediately before D.

Who teaches Biology?
qs.e: 1) C is on Wednesday. A and D are back-to-back with A first: Mon–Tue or Thu–Fri. 2) B (Drama) is on Tue or Thu. 3) If A–D were Mon–Tue, B would be Thu and E would be left with Friday — but Friday is English and E does not teach English. So A is Thu and D Fri (D teaches English). 4) B then takes Tue, and E Mon. 5) Art–Biology must be consecutive among Mon (E), Wed (C) and Thu (A): only Wed–Thu works. So C teaches Art, A Biology, and E Chemistry. Mon E Chemistry; Tue B Drama; Wed C Art; Thu A Biology; Fri D English. Biology: A.

qs.q:
Five teachers A, B, C, D and E each teach one class on a different day from Monday to Friday, and each teaches a different subject: Art, Biology, Chemistry, Drama or English.
• C teaches on Wednesday.
• The Biology class is on the day immediately after the Art class.
• B teaches Drama, but not on Monday or Friday.
• The English class is on Friday, and E does not teach English.
• A teaches on the day immediately before D.

Which subject is taught on Monday?
qs.e: 1) C is on Wednesday. A and D are back-to-back with A first: Mon–Tue or Thu–Fri. 2) B (Drama) is on Tue or Thu. 3) If A–D were Mon–Tue, B would be Thu and E would be left with Friday — but Friday is English and E does not teach English. So A is Thu and D Fri (D teaches English). 4) B then takes Tue, and E Mon. 5) Art–Biology must be consecutive among Mon (E), Wed (C) and Thu (A): only Wed–Thu works. So C teaches Art, A Biology, and E Chemistry. Mon E Chemistry; Tue B Drama; Wed C Art; Thu A Biology; Fri D English. Monday: Chemistry.

qs.q:
Five teachers A, B, C, D and E each teach one class on a different day from Monday to Friday, and each teaches a different subject: Art, Biology, Chemistry, Drama or English.
• C teaches on Wednesday.
• The Biology class is on the day immediately after the Art class.
• B teaches Drama, but not on Monday or Friday.
• The English class is on Friday, and E does not teach English.
• A teaches on the day immediately before D.

If only the first, third and fourth conditions above were given, in how many different ways could the teachers, days and subjects be matched?
qs.e:
Think it through with only three conditions: C on Wednesday; B teaches Drama on Tue or Thu; English is on Friday and is not taught by E.
1) B's day: 2 ways (Tue or Thu). 2) Friday's teacher: A or D, not E (whoever teaches Friday teaches English) — 2 ways. 3) The other two of A, D and E fill the two remaining days — 2 ways. People-to-days: 2 × 2 × 2 = 8.
4) Subjects: Drama (B) and English (Friday) are fixed; the remaining three subjects go to the remaining three teachers in 3 × 2 × 1 = 6 ways.
5) Total = 8 × 6 = 48.
Where mistakes happen: (a) 24 forgets that Friday can be A or D; (d) 120 ignores the conditions. This is a stretch item: counting arrangements under conditions, beyond what CSAT has asked.

qs.q:
Six boxes P, Q, R, S, T and U have different weights.
• P is heavier than Q, Q is heavier than S, S is heavier than R, and R is heavier than T.
• U is lighter than P but heavier than R.

Which one of the following is definitely true?
o: Exactly two boxes are lighter than U.
qs.e: Chain: P > Q > S > R > T. U lies somewhere below P and above R, so U can be in any of three places: between P and Q, between Q and S, or between S and R. Three orders are possible; only facts true in all three are 'definite'. U is above R and R is above T, so U is heavier than T in every order. (a), (c) and (d) each hold in only some orders.

qs.q:
Six boxes P, Q, R, S, T and U have different weights.
• P is heavier than Q, Q is heavier than S, S is heavier than R, and R is heavier than T.
• U is lighter than P but heavier than R.

How many boxes are definitely heavier than S?
qs.e: Chain: P > Q > S > R > T. U lies somewhere below P and above R, so U can be in any of three places: between P and Q, between Q and S, or between S and R. Three orders are possible; only facts true in all three are 'definite'. P and Q are always above S; U may be above or below S. So only two are definitely heavier.

qs.q:
Five people V, W, X, Y and Z sit in a row facing north.
• Exactly one person sits between V and X.
• W sits at one of the ends.
• Y sits immediately to the right of X.
These conditions allow more than one arrangement. Which one of the following additional conditions, together with those above, fixes the arrangement completely?
o: V sits somewhere to the left of X.
W sits at the right end.
Z sits in the middle of the row.
qs.e:
Think it through: 1) List all arrangements first. X–Y is a back-to-back pair with Y on the right; V is two places from X; W is at an end. Six rows are possible: V Z X Y W; W V Z X Y; X Y V Z W; W X Y V Z; Z X Y V W; W Z X Y V.
2) Test each extra condition: (d) Z in the middle (place 3) — only W V Z X Y. Unique. (b) V left of X — V Z X Y W and W V Z X Y: two remain. (c) W at the right end — V Z X Y W, X Y V Z W and Z X Y V W: three remain. (a) Z next to W — X Y V Z W and W Z X Y V: two remain.
Lesson: for 'which clue fixes it', list every arrangement first; then the right clue is the one that cuts the list to one. This is a stretch item.

qs.q: In a row of 41 children, A is 11th from the left end and B is 15th from the right end. If A and B exchange places, what will be A's position from the left end?
qs.e:
Think it through: A moves into B's place. B's place from the left = 41 − 15 + 1 = 27. So A becomes 27th from the left.
Where mistakes happen: (b) 26 forgets the +1; (a) 25 uses 41 − 15 − 1.

qs.q: In a class, P ranks 13th from the top. Q is 7 ranks below P, and Q ranks 21st from the bottom. How many students are in the class?
qs.e:
Think it through: 1) Q's rank from the top = 13 + 7 = 20. 2) Total = 20 + 21 − 1 = 40.
Where mistakes happen: (c) 41 forgets the −1; using P's rank with Q's bottom rank gives 33.

qs.q: In how many ways can six people A, B, C, D, E and F sit in a row if A and B must sit together and C must not sit at either end?
qs.e:
Think it through: 1) Treat A and B as one bundle: 5 units, which can be arranged in 5! = 120 ways, with 2 orders inside the bundle: 240 arrangements with A and B together.
2) Remove those with C at an end. C at the left end: the other 4 units (bundle + D, E, F) fill the rest in 4! × 2 = 48 ways. Same for the right end: 48.
3) 240 − 96 = 144.
Where mistakes happen: forgetting the factor 2 inside the bundle gives 72; removing only one end gives 192.

qs.q: In how many ways can four men and four women sit around a round table so that men and women sit alternately?
qs.e:
Think it through: 1) Seat the men first around the table: (4 − 1)! = 6 ways (rotations are the same). 2) Now there are 4 gaps between the men, one for each woman: 4! = 24 ways. 3) Total = 6 × 24 = 144.
Where mistakes happen: (c) 576 seats the men as if in a row (4! × 4!); (a) 72 also divides the women's count by a rotation that has already been removed.

csat-comprehension-l1.title: CSAT Module Test · Comprehension and Communication · Inference and Assumption · Level 1

qs.q: Which one of the following can be inferred from the passage?
o: Paddy should be banned in dry districts.
Paying farmers to switch crops may not work unless the new crops can be sold at a fair price.
Groundwater in dry districts will run out within a few years.
Millets earn farmers more money than paddy.
qs.e:
How to read these: an inference must follow from the passage; an assumption is something the author must take for granted — if you deny it, the argument falls. 
Evidence: the last sentence — a farmer will switch only if he is sure of a fair price for the new crop. So a payment to switch is not enough by itself: (b).
Why not the others: (a) is a strong step the passage never takes (extreme). (c) adds a time limit the passage does not give — it says only that wells go deeper (extreme). (d) compares incomes, which the passage does not discuss (out of scope).
qs.p: Many farmers in dry districts grow paddy because the government buys it at a fixed price. Paddy needs a lot of water. Where canals do not reach, farmers pump groundwater from deep wells, and each year the wells must go deeper. Some states now pay farmers who switch to millets or pulses. These crops need far less water. But a farmer will switch only if he is sure that he can sell the new crop at a fair price.

qs.q: The passage assumes that:
o: all farmers in dry districts grow paddy.
canals are the cheapest source of water for farmers.
farmers decide what to grow largely by what they expect to earn.
pulses grow well only in districts with plenty of water.
qs.e:
Test: deny the option and see if the passage still makes sense. If farmers did NOT care about earnings, a fixed price would not draw them to paddy, and a fair price would not decide whether they switch. The passage falls, so (c) is assumed.
Why not the others: (b) is never discussed (out of scope). (a) 'all' is too strong; the passage says 'many' (extreme). (d) contradicts the passage, which says pulses need far less water (opposite).
qs.p: Many farmers in dry districts grow paddy because the government buys it at a fixed price. Paddy needs a lot of water. Where canals do not reach, farmers pump groundwater from deep wells, and each year the wells must go deeper. Some states now pay farmers who switch to millets or pulses. These crops need far less water. But a farmer will switch only if he is sure that he can sell the new crop at a fair price.

qs.q: Which one of the following can be inferred from the passage?
o: Schools should ban phones in classrooms.
Children who use phones are always angry.
Cutting down screen use at night can help children learn better.
Lack of sleep is the main reason why children fail examinations.
qs.e:
Evidence: screens at night → less sleep → a tired child learns less. Remove the screens and the chain points the other way: better sleep, better learning. So (c) follows.
Why not the others: (b) 'always' goes far beyond 'gets angry more easily' (extreme). (a) is about classrooms; the passage talks about bedrooms at night (out of scope). (d) 'main reason' and 'fail' are never said (extreme).
qs.p: Doctors have noticed that many school children sleep less than they need. A common reason is the use of phones and tablets late at night. Bright screens tell the brain that it is still day, so the child finds it hard to fall asleep. A tired child learns less in class and gets angry more easily. Some schools now ask parents to keep devices out of the bedroom after dinner. Teachers in these schools say that students seem more alert in the morning.

qs.q: The teachers' report that students seem more alert in the morning is used to support the schools' step. This assumes that:
o: phones are more harmful than television.
parents in these schools agree with every school rule.
the change in alertness is due to keeping devices out of the bedroom.
children need as much sleep as adults.
qs.e:
Test: if the students were more alert for some other reason — say, a later school start — the teachers' report would not support the step. So the link between the step and the alertness is taken for granted: (c).
Why not the others: (b) 'every rule' is not needed (extreme). (a) and (d) bring in television and adults, which the passage never mentions (out of scope).
qs.p: Doctors have noticed that many school children sleep less than they need. A common reason is the use of phones and tablets late at night. Bright screens tell the brain that it is still day, so the child finds it hard to fall asleep. A tired child learns less in class and gets angry more easily. Some schools now ask parents to keep devices out of the bedroom after dinner. Teachers in these schools say that students seem more alert in the morning.

qs.q: Which one of the following can be inferred from the passage?
o: Cities should never widen their roads.
Planting saplings elsewhere does not at once replace the cooling lost when old trees are cut.
Saplings do not give off any water.
Trees are the only way to keep a city cool.
qs.e:
Evidence: old trees give shade and cool the air; a sapling takes many years to give the same shade. So for many years the loss is not made up: (b).
Why not the others: (a) 'never' is a ban the passage does not propose (extreme). (c) the passage says nothing about how much water saplings give off (out of scope). (d) 'only way' is too strong (extreme).
qs.p: On a hot afternoon, a street lined with trees can feel much cooler than a bare street nearby. Leaves block the sun before it reaches the road. They also give off water, which cools the air around them. Many cities cut old trees to widen roads. They plant young saplings elsewhere to make up for the loss. A sapling, however, takes many years to give the shade of a grown tree.

qs.q: Cities that plant saplings elsewhere to make up for cutting old trees seem to assume that:
o: the benefit lost by cutting trees can be restored by planting new ones.
wider roads make a city cooler.
old trees give very little shade.
saplings grow faster in cities than in villages.
qs.e:
Evidence: the words 'to make up for the loss' show what the cities believe — that new planting can restore what was lost. The passage then questions this belief. So (a) is the cities' assumption.
Why not the others: (b) nothing links road width to temperature (out of scope). (c) is the opposite of the passage. (d) compares cities and villages, which the passage never does (out of scope).
qs.p: On a hot afternoon, a street lined with trees can feel much cooler than a bare street nearby. Leaves block the sun before it reaches the road. They also give off water, which cools the air around them. Many cities cut old trees to widen roads. They plant young saplings elsewhere to make up for the loss. A sapling, however, takes many years to give the shade of a grown tree.

qs.q: Which one of the following can be inferred from the passage?
o: A record of digital payments can serve as proof of income for small sellers.
Tea sellers no longer accept cash.
Banks now lend to every small seller.
Digital payments have ended the shortage of coins in the country.
qs.e:
Evidence: banks did not lend because sellers had no proof of income; a record of daily sales can now help them get a loan. So the record works as proof of income: (a).
Why not the others: (b) the passage says 'many' sellers use the code, not that cash is refused (extreme). (c) 'every' is too strong; the record 'can help' (extreme). (d) the coin box is mentioned, not a national shortage (out of scope).
qs.p: A few years ago, a small tea seller had to keep a box of coins for change. Today many such sellers display a code that buyers scan with their phones. The money reaches the seller's bank account at once. Each payment also leaves a record. Banks were earlier unwilling to lend to such sellers because they had no proof of income. A record of daily sales can now help them get a loan.

qs.q: The passage assumes that banks:
o: do not trust cash payments at all.
charge lower interest on loans linked to digital payments.
prefer lending to large firms rather than small sellers.
are more willing to lend when they can see a borrower's income.
qs.e:
Test: if banks did not care about seeing income, a sales record would not help a seller get a loan. The passage depends on (d).
Why not the others: (b) interest rates are never mentioned (out of scope). (c) may well be true but the passage does not need it (true but not needed). (a) 'at all' is far too strong (extreme).
qs.p: A few years ago, a small tea seller had to keep a box of coins for change. Today many such sellers display a code that buyers scan with their phones. The money reaches the seller's bank account at once. Each payment also leaves a record. Banks were earlier unwilling to lend to such sellers because they had no proof of income. A record of daily sales can now help them get a loan.

qs.q: Which one of the following can be inferred from the passage?
o: Shopkeepers in the town still oppose the ban.
Cloth bags are cheaper than plastic bags.
The ban made no difference to the drains.
The ban reduced one cause of blocked drains but not all causes.
qs.e:
Evidence: fewer bags in the drains after the ban, but blockages continued from food packets and bottles, which the ban did not cover. So one cause fell, others remained: (d).
Why not the others: (b) prices are never discussed (out of scope). (c) is the opposite of 'fewer bags were seen in the drains'. (a) the passage says shopkeepers complained 'at first'; it does not say they still do (not supported).
qs.p: When a town banned thin plastic bags, many shoppers began carrying cloth bags. Shopkeepers complained at first. Within a year, fewer bags were seen in the drains, and the streets flooded less during the rains. Yet the drains still got blocked in some places. Officials found that these blockages came mostly from food packets and bottles, which the ban did not cover.

qs.q: The passage suggests that the streets flooded less because of the ban. For this to hold, it must be assumed that:
o: plastic bags were the only waste found in the drains.
the rains in that year were not much lighter than in earlier years.
all shoppers in the town now carry cloth bags.
food packets block drains more often than bottles do.
qs.e:
Test: if that year's rains were much lighter, the streets would have flooded less anyway, and the ban could not take the credit. So the link needs (b). This is a classic hidden assumption: ruling out another cause.
Why not the others: (a) contradicts the passage — packets and bottles were also found (opposite). (c) 'all' is not needed (extreme). (d) compares packets and bottles, which the passage does not do (out of scope).
qs.p: When a town banned thin plastic bags, many shoppers began carrying cloth bags. Shopkeepers complained at first. Within a year, fewer bags were seen in the drains, and the streets flooded less during the rains. Yet the drains still got blocked in some places. Officials found that these blockages came mostly from food packets and bottles, which the ban did not cover.

qs.q: Which one of the following can be inferred from the passage?
o: Children speak the same language at home and at school.
Children should never be taught a second language.
Teachers who use the home language are better trained.
A child's ability to repeat a lesson is not proof that she has understood it.
qs.e:
Evidence: a child may repeat words without knowing what they mean and 'seem to be doing well' yet fail to explain in her own words. So repeating is not the same as understanding: (d).
Why not the others: (b) the passage says 'first' taught in the home language; it does not reject a second language (extreme). (c) teacher training is not discussed (out of scope). (a) the passage is about cases where the two languages differ (opposite).
qs.p: Children often learn best when they are first taught in the language they speak at home. They understand what the teacher says and can ask questions freely. A child taught in an unfamiliar language may learn to repeat words without knowing what they mean. Such a child may seem to be doing well. She struggles, though, when asked to explain an idea in her own words.

qs.q: The author assumes that:
o: being able to ask questions freely helps a child learn.
the home language is always the official language of the state.
every child finds explaining harder than memorising.
qs.e:
Evidence: the author gives 'can ask questions freely' as a reason why children learn best in the home language. That reason works only if asking questions helps learning. So (a) is taken for granted.
Why not the others: (b) feelings about languages are not discussed (out of scope). (c) 'always' and 'official language' bring in something new (extreme, out of scope). (d) 'every child' is too strong (extreme).
qs.p: Children often learn best when they are first taught in the language they speak at home. They understand what the teacher says and can ask questions freely. A child taught in an unfamiliar language may learn to repeat words without knowing what they mean. Such a child may seem to be doing well. She struggles, though, when asked to explain an idea in her own words.

qs.q: Which one of the following can be inferred from the passage?
o: When a farmer sprays pesticide can affect the size of his own harvest.
Pesticides should be banned on farms.
All crops depend on bees for a good harvest.
Boxes of bees are too costly for most farmers.
qs.e:
Evidence: spraying at the wrong time kills bees, and bees improve the harvest of many crops. So the timing of spraying can change the harvest: (a).
Why not the others: (b) the passage suggests a better time, not a ban (extreme). (c) 'all crops' — the passage says 'many crops' (extreme). (d) cost is never mentioned (out of scope).
qs.p: Many crops, such as mustard and several fruits, give a better harvest when bees visit their flowers. Bees carry pollen from one flower to another. A farmer who sprays a strong pesticide at the wrong time can kill the very bees that help him. Some farmers now spray only in the evening, when fewer bees are out. Others keep boxes of bees near their fields.

qs.q: Farmers who spray only in the evening assume that:
o: pesticides do not work in daylight.
spraying when fewer bees are out will harm fewer bees.
bees never come out in the evening.
evening spraying gives a bigger harvest than keeping bee boxes.
qs.e:
Test: if spraying in the evening harmed as many bees as spraying by day, there would be no reason to wait for the evening. So (b) is the assumption.
Why not the others: (a) nothing is said about how well pesticides work (out of scope). (c) the passage says 'fewer bees', not none (extreme). (d) compares two methods the passage only lists (out of scope).
qs.p: Many crops, such as mustard and several fruits, give a better harvest when bees visit their flowers. Bees carry pollen from one flower to another. A farmer who sprays a strong pesticide at the wrong time can kill the very bees that help him. Some farmers now spray only in the evening, when fewer bees are out. Others keep boxes of bees near their fields.

qs.q: Which one of the following can be inferred from the passage?
o: A rise in the number of complaints does not by itself show that a problem has grown worse.
The old phone line was never used by residents.
The app has made the streetlights better.
Residents complain more than they need to.
qs.e:
Evidence: some officials read more complaints as worse streetlights; others point out that the app made complaining easier. Since both explanations fit, the count alone cannot settle it: (a).
Why not the others: (b) the old line received complaints, just fewer (extreme). (c) nothing is said about repairs (out of scope). (d) is a judgement the passage does not make (out of scope).
qs.p: A city asked residents to report broken streetlights through a phone app. Thousands of complaints came in during the first month, far more than the old phone line had ever received. Some officials concluded that the streetlights had become worse. Others pointed out that the app had simply made it easier to complain.

qs.q: The officials who concluded that the streetlights had become worse assumed that:
o: repair teams had become slower than before.
the app was not working properly.
residents prefer the app to the old phone line.
the number of complaints reflects the number of broken lights.
qs.e:
Test: if more complaints did NOT mean more broken lights, these officials would have no basis for their conclusion. So they must take (d) for granted.
Why not the others: (b) is the opposite — the app worked well enough to bring in thousands of complaints. (c) may be true, but their conclusion does not need it (true but not needed). (a) repair speed is not discussed (out of scope).
qs.p: A city asked residents to report broken streetlights through a phone app. Thousands of complaints came in during the first month, far more than the old phone line had ever received. Some officials concluded that the streetlights had become worse. Others pointed out that the app had simply made it easier to complain.

qs.q: Which one of the following can be inferred from the passage?
o: Old people prefer to live alone.
Joint families have disappeared in India.
Young people do not care about their parents.
Some of the support that old people once got at home now comes from outside the family.
qs.e:
Evidence: grandparents once lived with their families; now more live alone, and neighbours and local groups 'fill part of the gap'. So part of the support now comes from outside the family: (d).
Why not the others: (b) 'disappeared' is too strong; the passage says 'more' old people live alone (extreme). (c) is a judgement the passage never makes (out of scope). (a) preference is not discussed (out of scope).
qs.p: In many small towns, young people move to big cities for work. Their parents often stay behind in the family home. Earlier, grandparents usually lived with their children and grandchildren under one roof. Today, more old people live alone or with only a husband or wife. Neighbours and local groups have begun to fill part of the gap. They check in on the elderly and help with errands.

qs.q: The passage takes for granted that:
o: big cities offer no jobs to old people.
old people living alone may need help with daily tasks.
neighbours are better carers than family members.
all young people from small towns move to big cities.
qs.e:
Evidence: the passage calls the change a 'gap' and praises help with errands. That makes sense only if old people living alone may need such help: (b).
Why not the others: (a) jobs for old people are not discussed (out of scope). (c) compares carers, which the passage does not do (out of scope). (d) 'all' is too strong; the passage says 'many' (extreme).
qs.p: In many small towns, young people move to big cities for work. Their parents often stay behind in the family home. Earlier, grandparents usually lived with their children and grandchildren under one roof. Today, more old people live alone or with only a husband or wife. Neighbours and local groups have begun to fill part of the gap. They check in on the elderly and help with errands.

qs.q: Which one of the following best reflects the idea of the passage?
o: Quiet lanes should be closed to cars.
Online maps often give wrong directions.
Something that helps each user can cause harm when many people use it in the same way.
Drivers do not care about the people living along their route.
qs.e:
Evidence: each driver saves time, but when many follow the same advice, a quiet lane becomes unsafe. The last sentence says this directly: (c).
Why not the others: (b) the maps work as intended; the problem is crowding (opposite). (a) is a solution the passage does not offer (out of scope). (d) judges drivers' attitudes, which the passage does not discuss (out of scope).
qs.p: Online maps tell drivers the quickest way to reach a place. When many drivers follow the same advice, a quiet lane can suddenly fill with traffic. Residents of such lanes complain that their streets are no longer safe for children. A tool that saves time for each driver can create a new problem for the people who live along the route.

qs.q: The residents' complaint assumes that:
o: online maps should show lanes as closed.
more traffic in a lane makes it less safe for children.
drivers in lanes drive faster than on main roads.
qs.e:
Test: if more traffic did not make the lane less safe, the residents would have no complaint. So (c) is assumed.
Why not the others: (b) 'only' is too strong (extreme). (a) is a remedy, not an assumption (out of scope). (d) speed is never mentioned (out of scope).
qs.p: Online maps tell drivers the quickest way to reach a place. When many drivers follow the same advice, a quiet lane can suddenly fill with traffic. Residents of such lanes complain that their streets are no longer safe for children. A tool that saves time for each driver can create a new problem for the people who live along the route.

csat-comprehension-l2.title: CSAT Module Test · Comprehension and Communication · Inference and Assumption · Level 2

qs.q:
Consider the following statements:
1. Households with more information are better placed to protect the value of their savings.
2. Rising prices hurt only households that do not save.
Which of the above can be inferred from the passage?
qs.e:
