How to read these: an inference must follow from the passage; an assumption is something the author must take for granted — if you deny it, the argument falls. 
1 — valid. Households with more information move savings into other assets when bank interest lags behind prices; others rarely can. So they are better placed.
2 — invalid. The passage says every household may be saving and still fall behind; 'only those who do not save' contradicts it (opposite, extreme).
Answer: 1 only.
qs.p: When prices rise faster than the interest a bank pays on deposits, money held in an ordinary savings account slowly loses its value in real terms. A family that keeps its entire savings in such an account may discover, after several years of steady inflation, that the same savings purchase considerably less. Households with better access to financial information often shift part of their savings into other assets that are more likely to keep pace with prices. Those with less information, or with too little to save for such diversification to be worthwhile, rarely have that choice. A prolonged spell of high prices can therefore widen the gap between households, even when every one of them is saving.

qs.q: The passage most strongly suggests that:
o: banks should pay higher interest on savings accounts.
saving money is not enough by itself to protect a household against rising prices.
every household loses the same amount when prices rise.
other assets always grow faster than prices.
qs.e:
Evidence: money in a savings account 'slowly loses its value' when prices outrun interest, and the gap widens 'even when every one of them is saving'. Saving alone does not protect: (b).
Why not the others: (a) is a policy prescription the passage never makes (out of scope). (c) the passage says the gap widens — losses differ (opposite). (d) 'always' is never claimed (extreme).
qs.p: When prices rise faster than the interest a bank pays on deposits, money held in an ordinary savings account slowly loses its value in real terms. A family that keeps its entire savings in such an account may discover, after several years of steady inflation, that the same savings purchase considerably less. Households with better access to financial information often shift part of their savings into other assets that are more likely to keep pace with prices. Those with less information, or with too little to save for such diversification to be worthwhile, rarely have that choice. A prolonged spell of high prices can therefore widen the gap between households, even when every one of them is saving.

qs.q:
Consider the following statements:
1. A benefit that is hard to measure tends to be given less weight when land use is decided.
2. Fish farms earn more than any other use of coastal land.
Which of the above is/are assumed in the passage?
qs.e:
1 — assumed. The passage explains clearing 'because the land brings quick income while the protection ... is hard to put a price on'. That explanation works only if hard-to-price benefits get less weight.
2 — not assumed. The passage names fish farms and ports as uses; it never ranks them against all others ('any other' is extreme, out of scope).
Answer: 1 only.
qs.p: Mangrove forests along a coastline absorb much of the force of incoming waves before they reach the shore, and villages sheltered behind dense mangroves have frequently suffered less destruction during cyclones than settlements facing open beaches. Yet mangroves continue to be cleared for fish farms and port construction, because the land brings quick income while the protection the forest gives is hard to put a price on. The consequences of such clearing become visible only when a severe storm arrives, and by then the forest cannot be rebuilt in time.

qs.q: Which one of the following can be inferred from the passage?
o: Villages with open beaches can never be made safe from storms.
Decisions to clear mangroves may weigh present income more heavily than future safety.
Mangroves can be regrown within one storm season.
Ports should not be built along coasts.
qs.e:
Evidence: land is cleared for 'quick income'; the protection is noticed only when a storm comes. Present income wins over future safety: (b).
Why not the others: (a) 'never' goes beyond 'frequently suffered less destruction' behind mangroves (extreme). (c) contradicts 'cannot be rebuilt in time' (opposite). (d) is a recommendation the passage does not make (out of scope).
qs.p: Mangrove forests along a coastline absorb much of the force of incoming waves before they reach the shore, and villages sheltered behind dense mangroves have frequently suffered less destruction during cyclones than settlements facing open beaches. Yet mangroves continue to be cleared for fish farms and port construction, because the land brings quick income while the protection the forest gives is hard to put a price on. The consequences of such clearing become visible only when a severe storm arrives, and by then the forest cannot be rebuilt in time.

qs.q:
Consider the following statements:
1. Officials are less likely to misuse funds when they expect their decisions to be examined.
2. Publishing records has some effect even though it does not stop every misuse.
Which of the above can be inferred from the passage?
qs.e:
1 — valid. The rule works because officials 'are aware that their decisions may be read and questioned', which 'raises the cost of hiding' misuse.
2 — valid. It 'does not stop every misuse. But it raises the cost of hiding one' — a partial effect.
Answer: both.
Trap: students who see 'does not stop every misuse' may reject 2, reading partial as none.
qs.p: When a government office is required to publish details of how it spends public money, officials are aware that their decisions may be read and questioned by people outside the department. Disclosure of this kind does not stop every misuse. But it raises the cost of hiding one, since an irregular payment that appears in a published record can be traced, compared and challenged. A rule that makes records public works best when citizens, journalists or auditors actually read them; files that nobody opens deter very little.

qs.q: Which one of the following best captures the author's view of making government records public?
o: It should be replaced by stricter audits.
It is a complete remedy for the misuse of public money.
It is pointless, since officials still misuse funds.
It is a useful check, but its value depends on whether the records are actually read.
qs.e:
Evidence: it 'raises the cost' of hiding misuse (useful), and 'works best when citizens, journalists or auditors actually read them; files that nobody opens deter very little' (conditional). That is (d).
Why not the others: (b) the passage says it does not stop every misuse (extreme). (c) the author calls it useful, not pointless (opposite). (a) auditors are named as readers, not as a replacement (out of scope).
qs.p: When a government office is required to publish details of how it spends public money, officials are aware that their decisions may be read and questioned by people outside the department. Disclosure of this kind does not stop every misuse. But it raises the cost of hiding one, since an irregular payment that appears in a published record can be traced, compared and challenged. A rule that makes records public works best when citizens, journalists or auditors actually read them; files that nobody opens deter very little.

qs.q:
Consider the following statements:
1. Bacteria become resistant because the antibiotic changes them.
2. Unnecessary use of antibiotics by some people can affect the treatment of others.
Which of the above can be inferred from the passage?
qs.e:
1 — invalid. The passage says survivors 'may carry traits that let them resist the drug' and pass them on. The drug picks out bacteria that already resist; it does not change them (reversed relation).
2 — valid. Needless use gives hardy bacteria 'another chance to spread', and the medicine 'may thus fail many patients later'.
Answer: 2 only.
qs.p: Antibiotics destroy most of the bacteria responsible for an infection, but seldom eliminate every one of them. The few that survive a course of treatment may carry traits that let them resist the drug, and they pass these traits on as they multiply, so that each later generation contains a larger proportion of resistant organisms. Each time an antibiotic is taken when it is not needed, as for a common cold caused by a virus, the hardy bacteria get another chance to spread. A medicine that cures one patient today may thus fail many patients later.

qs.q: The author's example of the common cold rests on the assumption that:
o: resistant bacteria cannot spread from one person to another.
every cold leads to a bacterial infection.
an antibiotic does not cure a cold caused by a virus.
qs.e:
Evidence: the cold is offered as a case where the antibiotic 'is not needed'. That holds only if the drug does nothing against the viral cold: (d).
Why not the others: (b) is the opposite of the example's point (opposite). (c) contradicts the idea of needless use (opposite). (a) contradicts 'get another chance to spread' (opposite).
qs.p: Antibiotics destroy most of the bacteria responsible for an infection, but seldom eliminate every one of them. The few that survive a course of treatment may carry traits that let them resist the drug, and they pass these traits on as they multiply, so that each later generation contains a larger proportion of resistant organisms. Each time an antibiotic is taken when it is not needed, as for a common cold caused by a virus, the hardy bacteria get another chance to spread. A medicine that cures one patient today may thus fail many patients later.

qs.q:
Consider the following statements:
1. Lower fares alone may not persuade car owners to travel by bus.
2. Faster and less crowded buses would certainly reduce traffic on the main roads.
Which of the above can be inferred from the passage?
qs.e:
1 — valid. Fares fell, few car owners switched, and price 'had never been the main concern' for them.
2 — invalid. The passage says car owners care about time and crowding, but 'certainly reduce traffic' is a prediction it cannot support (extreme).
Answer: 1 only.
qs.p: A metropolitan transport authority reduced bus fares substantially in an attempt to persuade commuters to leave their cars at home. The number of bus passengers increased noticeably, but congestion on the principal arterial roads barely eased. A subsequent survey revealed that most new riders had earlier walked, cycled or shared autorickshaws; very few had given up a car. For car owners, the price of the trip had never been the main concern. What mattered to them was the duration of the journey and the likelihood of finding the bus uncomfortably crowded.

qs.q: The rise in the number of bus riders after the fare cut is best explained by:
o: people who used to walk, cycle or share autorickshaws moving to buses.
car owners giving up their cars.
the city adding more buses on busy routes.
the main roads becoming less crowded.
qs.e:
Evidence: the survey found 'most new riders had earlier walked, cycled or shared autorickshaws'. That explains the rise: (a).
Why not the others: (b) the survey says few gave up a car (opposite). (c) new buses are never mentioned (out of scope). (d) traffic 'barely eased' — and it would be a result, not a cause (reversed, opposite).
qs.p: A metropolitan transport authority reduced bus fares substantially in an attempt to persuade commuters to leave their cars at home. The number of bus passengers increased noticeably, but congestion on the principal arterial roads barely eased. A subsequent survey revealed that most new riders had earlier walked, cycled or shared autorickshaws; very few had given up a car. For car owners, the price of the trip had never been the main concern. What mattered to them was the duration of the journey and the likelihood of finding the bus uncomfortably crowded.

qs.q:
Consider the following statements:
1. Teachers and students adjust what they do to what an examination rewards.
2. The kind of questions asked in an examination can change how students prepare.
Which of the above is/are assumed in the passage?
qs.e:
1 — assumed. The whole argument rests on teachers and coaching centres shaping lessons 'around what the examination is likely to ask'.
2 — assumed. The conclusion 'It has to change the questions' works only if changing questions changes preparation.
Answer: both.
Trap: statement 2 sounds like the conclusion, so students drop it — but a conclusion's premise that 'questions shape preparation' is exactly what is assumed.
qs.p: Examinations that reward the recall of information encourage students to memorise; examinations that reward analysis encourage them to reason. Teachers understand this connection, and so do coaching institutions, and both consequently organise their instruction around what the examination is likely to ask rather than around what the syllabus formally prescribes. If an examining board genuinely wants its students to think, changing the syllabus is not enough. It has to change the questions.

qs.q: Which one of the following can be inferred from the passage?
o: Coaching centres oppose examinations based on reasoning.
A new syllabus examined through old-style questions may leave students' study habits unchanged.
Changing the syllabus serves no purpose at all.
qs.e:
Evidence: 'changing the syllabus is not enough. It has to change the questions.' If the questions stay the same, preparation stays the same: (c).
Why not the others: (b) coaching centres adapt; they are not said to oppose (out of scope). (a) preference is not discussed (out of scope). (d) 'not enough' is not 'no purpose' (extreme).
qs.p: Examinations that reward the recall of information encourage students to memorise; examinations that reward analysis encourage them to reason. Teachers understand this connection, and so do coaching institutions, and both consequently organise their instruction around what the examination is likely to ask rather than around what the syllabus formally prescribes. If an examining board genuinely wants its students to think, changing the syllabus is not enough. It has to change the questions.

qs.q:
Consider the following statements:
1. Lantana is harmful to forests only because it catches fire easily.
2. Lantana was brought to India to provide food for deer.
Which of the above can be inferred from the passage?
qs.e:
1 — invalid. Fire is one of three harms; it also grows fast and crowds out grasses ('only' is a partial truth made extreme).
2 — invalid. Lantana came 'as a garden plant', and it crowds out the grasses deer eat (out of scope, opposite).
Answer: neither.
qs.p: Lantana, an ornamental shrub introduced into India as a garden plant during the colonial period, has since spread across large areas of many forests. It grows rapidly, suppresses the grasses on which deer and other herbivores depend, and increases the intensity of forest fires because its dry stems ignite easily. Clearing it is expensive and labour-intensive, and it returns within a few seasons unless the cleared land is planted with native species. Forest managers have therefore learned that removal without replanting is often money wasted.

qs.q: The forest managers' lesson that removal without replanting is often money wasted assumes that:
o: grasses grow back by themselves once lantana is removed.
planting native species costs more than clearing lantana.
lantana cannot be cleared by any method.
money spent on clearing lantana is lost if the shrub grows back.
qs.e:
Test: if clearing kept its value even after lantana returned, removal without replanting would not be 'money wasted'. So (d) is assumed.
Why not the others: (b) costs are not compared (out of scope). (c) contradicts the passage — it can be cleared, at a cost (opposite). (a) contradicts the point that lantana returns unless native species are planted (opposite).
qs.p: Lantana, an ornamental shrub introduced into India as a garden plant during the colonial period, has since spread across large areas of many forests. It grows rapidly, suppresses the grasses on which deer and other herbivores depend, and increases the intensity of forest fires because its dry stems ignite easily. Clearing it is expensive and labour-intensive, and it returns within a few seasons unless the cleared land is planted with native species. Forest managers have therefore learned that removal without replanting is often money wasted.

qs.q:
Consider the following statements:
1. All free apps sell their users' data.
2. A service can have a cost even when no money is charged for it.
Which of the above can be inferred from the passage?
qs.e:
1 — invalid. The passage says the company 'often' earns from data; 'all' and 'sell' go beyond it (extreme).
2 — valid. 'The real price of such a service is paid not in money but in information.'
Answer: 2 only.
qs.p: A complimentary fitness application that records a person's daily walk may appear to cost its users nothing. The company that operates it, however, often earns by studying the data its users generate: where they travel, when they sleep, what they purchase, and how these habits change over time. Users seldom examine the lengthy terms and conditions they accept before installing such software. The real price of such a service is paid not in money but in information, and most users have little idea how much they have paid.

qs.q: Which one of the following is an assumption on which the passage rests?
o: Companies always misuse the data they collect.
Users would stop using such apps if they read the terms.
Walking apps are less safe than other apps.
Information about a person's habits is of value to others.
qs.e:
Test: if information about where people go and what they buy were worth nothing, it could not be the 'real price' of the service, and companies could not earn from it. So (d) is assumed.
Why not the others: (b) predicts behaviour the passage does not discuss (out of scope). (c) compares apps (out of scope). (a) 'always misuse' goes far beyond 'earns by studying' (extreme).
qs.p: A complimentary fitness application that records a person's daily walk may appear to cost its users nothing. The company that operates it, however, often earns by studying the data its users generate: where they travel, when they sleep, what they purchase, and how these habits change over time. Users seldom examine the lengthy terms and conditions they accept before installing such software. The real price of such a service is paid not in money but in information, and most users have little idea how much they have paid.

qs.q:
Consider the following statements:
1. A rise in average income does not show that most people have become richer.
2. Clean air and safe neighbourhoods are more valuable than income.
Which of the above can be inferred from the passage?
qs.e:
1 — valid. 'A large gain for a few can lift the average even if most incomes stand still.'
2 — invalid. The passage says income leaves out things people value; it does not rank them above income (out of scope).
Answer: 1 only.
qs.p: A country's national income can rise steadily while a large proportion of its population feels no better off. Average income is simply a total divided by the number of people, and a large gain for a few can lift the average even if most incomes stand still. National income accounts also omit much that people value, including clean air, safe neighbourhoods and leisure time spent with family. The figure is useful for many purposes, but it answers a narrower question than the one people usually ask of it.

qs.q: The 'narrower question' that average income answers is best described as:
o: how fairly income is shared among people.
how happy people in the country are.
how much is earned in total, spread across each person.
how fast prices are rising in the country.
qs.e:
Evidence: average income is 'a total divided by the number of people' — that is what it measures. The broader question people ask of it is whether they are better off.
Why not the others: (b) is the broader question, not the narrow one (opposite). (a) the passage shows the average hides how income is shared (opposite). (d) prices are not discussed (out of scope).
qs.p: A country's national income can rise steadily while a large proportion of its population feels no better off. Average income is simply a total divided by the number of people, and a large gain for a few can lift the average even if most incomes stand still. National income accounts also omit much that people value, including clean air, safe neighbourhoods and leisure time spent with family. The figure is useful for many purposes, but it answers a narrower question than the one people usually ask of it.

qs.q:
Consider the following statements:
1. A single dry day cannot show that a seventy per cent forecast of rain was wrong.
2. A forecaster whose seventy per cent days stay dry about three times in ten is doing well.
Which of the above can be inferred from the passage?
qs.e:
1 — valid. 'On that evidence alone, it was not' wrong.
2 — valid. A seventy per cent forecast means rain about seven times in ten; dry three times in ten is what a good forecast predicts.
Answer: both.
Trap: statement 2 sounds like praise for being wrong three times in ten — but by the passage's definition that is being right.
qs.p: When a meteorological office announces a seventy per cent probability of rain for the following day and the day then remains dry, many people conclude that the forecast was mistaken. On that evidence alone, it was not. A probabilistic forecast of this kind means that, on days with similar atmospheric conditions, rain falls on roughly seven occasions out of ten. To evaluate the forecaster fairly, one has to look at many such days, not one.

qs.q: The author's method of judging a forecaster assumes that:
o: rain is more likely in the evening than in the morning.
there are enough similar days to compare the forecasts with what actually happened.
most people understand chances and probabilities well.
forecasts of seventy per cent always turn out to be right.
qs.e:
Test: the method is to 'look at many such days'. If there were not enough similar days, the method could not be used. So (b) is assumed.
Why not the others: (a) time of day is never mentioned (out of scope). (c) the passage suggests the opposite — people misread the forecast (opposite). (d) 'always right' misreads the idea of a chance (extreme).
qs.p: When a meteorological office announces a seventy per cent probability of rain for the following day and the day then remains dry, many people conclude that the forecast was mistaken. On that evidence alone, it was not. A probabilistic forecast of this kind means that, on days with similar atmospheric conditions, rain falls on roughly seven occasions out of ten. To evaluate the forecaster fairly, one has to look at many such days, not one.

csat-comprehension-l3.title: CSAT Module Test · Comprehension and Communication · Inference and Assumption · Level 3

qs.q:
Consider the following statements:
1. The behaviour described in the passage can occur among people acting in good faith.
2. Measurement should be given up wherever it creates incentives.
3. Hospitals and schools are judged more harshly than other institutions.
Which of the above can be inferred from the passage?
qs.e:
How to read these: an inference must follow from the passage; an assumption is something the author must take for granted — if you deny it, the argument falls. 
1 — valid. 'None of this requires dishonesty; it requires only that people respond, sensibly enough, to the incentives.'
2 — invalid. 'The lesson is not that measurement is futile' — the passage rejects this (opposite).
3 — invalid. Hospitals and schools are examples; no comparison with other institutions is made (out of scope).
Answer: 1 only.
qs.p: When a performance indicator becomes an explicit target, the individuals and institutions being evaluated tend to learn how to move the indicator itself rather than the underlying condition it was originally intended to reflect. A hospital judged by how quickly it discharges patients may discharge them sooner, and see more of them return; a school rated principally on its pass percentage may quietly discourage academically weaker students from sitting the examination at all. None of this requires dishonesty; it requires only that people respond, sensibly enough, to the incentives placed before them. The lesson is not that measurement is futile, but that any single quantitative indicator, once systematically rewarded, begins to drift away from the phenomenon it was chosen to capture.

qs.q: The example of the hospital is used mainly to show that:
o: hospitals tend to be dishonest about their records.
a reported figure can improve while the outcome it stands for gets worse.
the speed of discharge is a poor measure for every kind of hospital.
patients return because doctors are careless.
qs.e:
Evidence: the hospital discharges patients sooner (the figure improves) and 'see more of them return' (the outcome worsens). That illustrates the opening claim: (b).
Why not the others: (a) the passage says 'none of this requires dishonesty' (opposite). (c) 'every kind of hospital' generalises far beyond one example (extreme, too broad). (d) blames doctors' care, which is not discussed (out of scope).
qs.p: When a performance indicator becomes an explicit target, the individuals and institutions being evaluated tend to learn how to move the indicator itself rather than the underlying condition it was originally intended to reflect. A hospital judged by how quickly it discharges patients may discharge them sooner, and see more of them return; a school rated principally on its pass percentage may quietly discourage academically weaker students from sitting the examination at all. None of this requires dishonesty; it requires only that people respond, sensibly enough, to the incentives placed before them. The lesson is not that measurement is futile, but that any single quantitative indicator, once systematically rewarded, begins to drift away from the phenomenon it was chosen to capture.

qs.q:
Consider the following statements:
1. Farmers would hold back their crop after harvest if they could afford to wait.
2. Cold stores will have no effect on onion prices.
Which of the above is/are assumed in the passage?
qs.e:
1 — assumed. The argument is that storage fails the farmer because he 'must repay a loan at harvest'. That works only if, free of that pressure, he would wait — deny it, and credit would not help.
2 — not assumed. The passage says cold stores 'may smooth prices for consumers' (opposite).
Answer: 1 only.
qs.p: Onion prices in India fluctuate dramatically across the agricultural calendar: an abundance immediately after harvest depresses them, while scarcity during the months preceding the subsequent crop drives them sharply upwards. Improved storage infrastructure would appear to offer an obvious remedy, enabling cultivators to retain their produce and sell once prices have recovered. Storage, however, benefits only those who can afford to wait. A farmer who must repay a loan at harvest sells immediately, whatever the prevailing price, while a trader with capital buys his crop and stores it until the market turns. Unless institutional credit reaches the cultivator himself, cold-storage capacity may smooth prices for consumers while leaving the grower's share much as it was.

qs.q: Which one of the following follows most directly from the passage?
o: Building cold stores is a waste of public money.
Storage may mainly benefit those who have the money to hold stock, not necessarily the grower.
Onion prices are controlled by traders.
Giving credit to farmers will put an end to swings in onion prices.
qs.e:
Evidence: the trader 'with capital buys his crop and stores it'; without credit, storage leaves 'the grower's share much as it was'. Whoever can afford to wait gains: (b).
Why not the others: (a) storage helps consumers, says the passage — not a waste (extreme, opposite). (c) 'controlled' is far stronger than anything said (extreme). (d) credit helps the farmer's share; ending price swings is a much larger claim (extreme).
qs.p: Onion prices in India fluctuate dramatically across the agricultural calendar: an abundance immediately after harvest depresses them, while scarcity during the months preceding the subsequent crop drives them sharply upwards. Improved storage infrastructure would appear to offer an obvious remedy, enabling cultivators to retain their produce and sell once prices have recovered. Storage, however, benefits only those who can afford to wait. A farmer who must repay a loan at harvest sells immediately, whatever the prevailing price, while a trader with capital buys his crop and stores it until the market turns. Unless institutional credit reaches the cultivator himself, cold-storage capacity may smooth prices for consumers while leaving the grower's share much as it was.

qs.q:
Consider the following statements:
1. Features of a household other than books can affect children's reading.
2. Books have no effect on children's reading scores.
3. The study did not separate the effect of books from that of other household features.
Which of the above are assumptions made by the author?
qs.e:
1 — assumed. The whole doubt rests on other features (reading parents, talk, quiet) possibly driving scores.
2 — not assumed. The author expects 'smaller gains', not none (extreme).
3 — assumed. If the study had already separated books from these features, the author's doubt would have no force. Deny 3 and the argument falls.
Answer: 1 and 3 only.
Trap: 2 tempts readers who turn 'not the whole cause' into 'no cause'.
qs.p: A widely reported study finds that children who own more books obtain higher scores on standardised reading assessments, and it is tempting to conclude that distributing books to children will, by itself, raise their scores. Households that possess many books, however, may differ systematically in other respects: parents who read habitually themselves, more extended conversation between adults and children, and quieter domestic surroundings in which to study. The books may therefore be a symptom of such a household rather than the cause of its children's reading ability, and a programme that merely delivers books to homes lacking these characteristics may produce considerably smaller gains than the study appears to promise.

qs.q: Which one of the following, if true, would most weaken the author's argument?
o: Reading scores differ widely from one school to another.
Families that own many books also tend to have higher incomes.
Children in homes that were given free books improved their scores as much as the study had predicted.
Some parents who own many books rarely read to their children.
qs.e:
How to weaken: the author says books may be a symptom, not a cause, so a book programme may disappoint. Direct evidence that delivered books DID produce the predicted gains hits that claim head-on: (c).
Why not the others: (b) adds another household difference — it supports the author (strengthens). (a) is about schools, not books at home (out of scope). (d) is a scattered case that hardly bears on the average effect (irrelevant, too narrow).
This is a stretch item: CSAT has used inference and assumption stems, not 'weaken' stems.
qs.p: A widely reported study finds that children who own more books obtain higher scores on standardised reading assessments, and it is tempting to conclude that distributing books to children will, by itself, raise their scores. Households that possess many books, however, may differ systematically in other respects: parents who read habitually themselves, more extended conversation between adults and children, and quieter domestic surroundings in which to study. The books may therefore be a symptom of such a household rather than the cause of its children's reading ability, and a programme that merely delivers books to homes lacking these characteristics may produce considerably smaller gains than the study appears to promise.

qs.q:
Consider the following statements:
1. Knowing a local problem well does not by itself ensure the ability to solve it.
2. Giving local bodies responsibility without resources may make them appear to fail.
Which of the above can be inferred from the passage?
qs.e:
1 — valid. The council 'may know exactly which well runs dry ... and still be unable to act'.
2 — valid. Such decentralisation 'can leave local bodies blamed for failures they were never equipped to prevent'.
Answer: both.
qs.p: The transfer of decision-making to local bodies is commonly defended on the ground that people closest to a problem understand it best. That argument is frequently true of knowledge, and considerably less often true of power. A village council may know exactly which well runs dry each summer and still be unable to act, because sanctioned funds arrive late, its technical staff answer to a distant line department rather than to the council, or a handful of influential families dominate its deliberations. Decentralisation that transfers responsibility without commensurate financial and administrative authority can leave local bodies blamed for failures they were never equipped to prevent.

qs.q: The author's attitude towards decentralisation is best described as:
o: accepting its basic reasoning but doubtful about the way it is often carried out.
opposed to it, because local bodies lack knowledge of local problems.
fully confident that it improves local government.
indifferent to whether it succeeds or fails.
qs.e:
Evidence: the author grants the premise ('frequently true of knowledge') and then shows how it fails in practice when money and authority do not follow. That is (a).
Why not the others: (b) reverses the passage — local bodies have the knowledge but lack power (reversed). (c) ignores the warning (extreme). (d) the author clearly cares about the outcome (opposite).
qs.p: The transfer of decision-making to local bodies is commonly defended on the ground that people closest to a problem understand it best. That argument is frequently true of knowledge, and considerably less often true of power. A village council may know exactly which well runs dry each summer and still be unable to act, because sanctioned funds arrive late, its technical staff answer to a distant line department rather than to the council, or a handful of influential families dominate its deliberations. Decentralisation that transfers responsibility without commensurate financial and administrative authority can leave local bodies blamed for failures they were never equipped to prevent.

qs.q:
Consider the following statements:
1. Skills that are rarely used may decline.
2. Automated systems should be removed from aircraft.
3. Automation makes emergencies more frequent.
Which of the above can be inferred from the passage?
qs.e:
1 — valid. Less hand-flying means less practice; the pilot's skills are 'least fresh' when needed.
2 — invalid. The passage describes a risk; it proposes no removal (out of scope, extreme).
3 — invalid. The passage says humans are needed less often, not that emergencies become more frequent (reversed).
Answer: 1 only.
qs.p: Pilots who rely on automated flight-management systems for the greater part of a journey accumulate correspondingly less experience of flying the aircraft manually. When the automation fails, usually in unusual conditions, the pilot must assume control at precisely the moment when the situation is most demanding and his own skills are least fresh. An analogous pattern appears wherever machines take over routine operations and leave human operators responsible only for infrequent emergencies. The better the automation, the less often the human is needed, and the less ready he may be when he is.

qs.q: Which one of the following can be most reasonably inferred from the passage?
o: Pilots today are less skilled than pilots before automation.
Making automation more reliable can make the rare human takeover more risky.
Automated systems fail mostly in routine conditions.
Machines should be designed to handle emergencies as well.
qs.e:
Evidence: 'The better the automation, the less often the human is needed, and the less ready he may be when he is.' So improving automation can raise the risk at the moment of takeover: (b).
Why not the others: (a) compares generations of pilots in general — the passage speaks of hand-flying practice only (extreme, too broad). (c) the passage says failures come 'usually in unusual conditions' (opposite). (d) is a design proposal the passage does not make (out of scope).
qs.p: Pilots who rely on automated flight-management systems for the greater part of a journey accumulate correspondingly less experience of flying the aircraft manually. When the automation fails, usually in unusual conditions, the pilot must assume control at precisely the moment when the situation is most demanding and his own skills are least fresh. An analogous pattern appears wherever machines take over routine operations and leave human operators responsible only for infrequent emergencies. The better the automation, the less often the human is needed, and the less ready he may be when he is.

qs.q: The claim that the neighbour 'can sell more cheaply' rests on the assumption that:
o: the honest shopkeeper charges more than the goods are worth.
customers always buy from the cheapest seller.
a trader who saves on tax can pass part of that saving on as lower prices.
traders who evade tax are never caught.
qs.e:
Test: if the money saved by evading tax could not be used to lower prices, the neighbour could not undercut the honest shopkeeper. So (c) is assumed.
Why not the others: (b) the argument needs customers to respond to price, not 'always' to buy the cheapest (extreme — the trap closest to the key). (a) the honest seller's prices are not called unfair (out of scope). (d) 'never caught' is not needed; evasion only has to be easy (extreme).
qs.p: A tax that is easily evaded ultimately penalises precisely those individuals who conscientiously comply with it. If one shopkeeper pays the full amount due while his neighbour conceals part of his turnover, the neighbour can sell more cheaply and gradually draw away the honest trader's customers. Over a period of years, honesty consequently becomes a competitive disadvantage in the marketplace rather than a virtue that costs its possessor nothing. Simplifying a tax and making it harder to dodge is therefore not only a matter of collecting revenue; it is also a matter of fairness between those who pay and those who do not.

qs.q: The passage implies that a simpler tax that is harder to evade:
o: will put an end to tax evasion.
can serve fairness as well as revenue.
is fair only to large traders.
qs.e:
Evidence: 'not only a matter of collecting revenue; it is also a matter of fairness between those who pay and those who do not' — (b).
Why not the others: (a) 'harder to dodge' is not 'ends evasion' (extreme). (c) large traders are not discussed (out of scope). (d) contradicts 'collecting revenue' (opposite).
qs.p: A tax that is easily evaded ultimately penalises precisely those individuals who conscientiously comply with it. If one shopkeeper pays the full amount due while his neighbour conceals part of his turnover, the neighbour can sell more cheaply and gradually draw away the honest trader's customers. Over a period of years, honesty consequently becomes a competitive disadvantage in the marketplace rather than a virtue that costs its possessor nothing. Simplifying a tax and making it harder to dodge is therefore not only a matter of collecting revenue; it is also a matter of fairness between those who pay and those who do not.

qs.q:
Consider the following statements:
1. The value of an added solar panel depends partly on when its power is needed.
2. Adding solar panels alone can make the midday surplus larger.
3. A grid with a large share of solar capacity can face both a surplus and a shortage on the same day.
Which of the above can be inferred from the passage?
qs.e:
1 — valid. Extra panels widen the midday surplus that cannot be used, so their value depends on timing.
2 — valid. 'Adding more panels does not close this gap; it widens the midday surplus.'
3 — valid. 'more electricity than it can use at noon and too little a few hours later'.
Answer: 1, 2 and 3.
Trap: students expect at least one statement to be false and drop 1 because it is not stated in so many words.
qs.p: Photovoltaic installations generate the greater part of their output around midday, whereas residential electricity consumption in many Indian cities reaches its maximum during the evening. On a sunny day, therefore, a grid with a substantial share of solar capacity may have more electricity than it can use at noon and too little a few hours later, when lighting and cooling loads rise. Adding more panels does not close this gap; it widens the midday surplus. What closes it is storage, consumption that can be deliberately shifted into the afternoon, or dispatchable generating capacity that can be brought online as the sun goes down.

qs.q: The claim that adding panels 'widens the midday surplus' assumes that:
o: cities use no electricity at noon.
evening demand for electricity will fall.
storage of electricity is too costly to be used.
the added panels also produce most of their power around midday.
qs.e:
Test: if the new panels produced their power in the evening, they would close the gap, not widen the surplus. So (d) is assumed.
Why not the others: (b) is not needed and not suggested (out of scope). (c) the passage names storage as a solution (opposite). (a) 'no electricity' is extreme; the passage speaks of a surplus, not zero use.
qs.p: Photovoltaic installations generate the greater part of their output around midday, whereas residential electricity consumption in many Indian cities reaches its maximum during the evening. On a sunny day, therefore, a grid with a substantial share of solar capacity may have more electricity than it can use at noon and too little a few hours later, when lighting and cooling loads rise. Adding more panels does not close this gap; it widens the midday surplus. What closes it is storage, consumption that can be deliberately shifted into the afternoon, or dispatchable generating capacity that can be brought online as the sun goes down.

qs.q:
Consider the following statements:
1. Fixed rules prevent all corruption by officials.
2. Most systems have settled how much room for exceptions to allow.
Which of the above can be inferred from the passage?
qs.e:
1 — invalid. Rules make favour harder to accuse, but 'all corruption' goes far beyond (extreme).
2 — invalid. Systems 'argue for ever about how wide the door should be' — the question is not settled (opposite).
Answer: neither.
qs.p: Fixed rules treat similar cases alike and are easy to verify; an official who applies them faithfully cannot easily be accused of favouritism. No rulebook, however, anticipates every circumstance, and a rule applied to a situation for which it was never designed can produce consequences that nobody intended. Discretion permits an official to tailor the decision to the particular case, at the price of making it considerably harder to distinguish a judicious exception from a corrupt one. Most administrative systems eventually settle on rules with a narrow door for exceptions, and then argue for ever about how wide the door should be.

qs.q: In the passage, the 'narrow door' refers to:
o: limited room for officials to depart from rules in special cases.
a strict ban on all exceptions to rules.
the difficulty of being appointed as an official.
the failure of rulebooks to foresee every case.
qs.e:
Evidence: systems 'settle on rules with a narrow door for exceptions' — the door is the opening for exceptions, and narrow means limited: (a).
Why not the others: (b) a narrow door is still a door — not a ban (opposite). (c) appointments are not discussed (out of scope). (d) is the reason a door is needed, not the door itself (partial).
qs.p: Fixed rules treat similar cases alike and are easy to verify; an official who applies them faithfully cannot easily be accused of favouritism. No rulebook, however, anticipates every circumstance, and a rule applied to a situation for which it was never designed can produce consequences that nobody intended. Discretion permits an official to tailor the decision to the particular case, at the price of making it considerably harder to distinguish a judicious exception from a corrupt one. Most administrative systems eventually settle on rules with a narrow door for exceptions, and then argue for ever about how wide the door should be.

qs.q:
Consider the following statements:
1. A finding becomes settled knowledge once it is published.
2. Surprising findings usually result from dishonesty.
3. Public belief in a finding may run ahead of the evidence for it.
Which of the above can be inferred from the passage?
qs.e:
1 — invalid. An unrepeated finding is 'closer to a promising lead than to settled knowledge' (opposite).
2 — invalid. The passage lists small samples, chance and 'honest errors' (opposite).
3 — valid. The public 'may therefore end up more certain than the scientists'.
Answer: 3 only.
qs.p: A single striking investigation attracts considerable publicity, whereas the painstaking and unglamorous work of attempting to reproduce it rarely does. Yet a finding that independent researchers have not reproduced is closer to a promising lead than to settled knowledge, since small samples, chance correlations and honest errors of method all generate surprising results that subsequently fade. The public, which hears of the first study and seldom of the attempts to repeat it, may therefore end up more certain than the scientists who did the work.

qs.q: The last sentence of the passage assumes that:
o: news outlets deliberately hide failed repetitions.
scientists never trust a study until it is repeated.
attempts to repeat a study are themselves always correct.
the public forms its view of scientific findings largely from what is reported.
qs.e:
Test: the public becomes over-certain because it 'hears of the first study and seldom of the attempts to repeat it'. That reasoning works only if what the public hears shapes what it believes. Deny (d) and the conclusion falls.
Why not the others: (b) 'never' is too strong (extreme). (c) 'always correct' is not needed (extreme). (a) 'deliberately' adds a motive the passage does not give (out of scope).
qs.p: A single striking investigation attracts considerable publicity, whereas the painstaking and unglamorous work of attempting to reproduce it rarely does. Yet a finding that independent researchers have not reproduced is closer to a promising lead than to settled knowledge, since small samples, chance correlations and honest errors of method all generate surprising results that subsequently fade. The public, which hears of the first study and seldom of the attempts to repeat it, may therefore end up more certain than the scientists who did the work.

qs.q:
Consider the following statements:
1. Translators often have to choose which feature of the original to keep.
2. A perfect translation of any sentence is possible with enough skill.
3. The meaning of a sentence cannot always be fully separated from its words.
Which of the above can be inferred from the passage?
qs.e:
1 — valid. Translators describe the work as 'a sequence of choices among losses'; a pun keeps sound or sense.
2 — invalid. 'The question is seldom whether something will be lost' — loss is normal (opposite).
3 — valid. The author treats as mistaken the idea that sense exists 'independently of the particular words that carry it'; the examples show meaning tied to words.
Answer: 1 and 3 only.
qs.p: Translation is commonly imagined as the transfer of a fixed meaning from one linguistic container to another, as though the sense of a sentence existed independently of the particular words that carry it. Experienced professional translators characteristically describe their activity rather differently, as a sequence of choices among losses: a pun can preserve its sound or its sense but rarely both, and a formal register in one language may have no counterpart in another that does not sound either stilted or casual. The question is seldom whether something will be lost, but which loss the reader of the translation can best afford.

qs.q: Which one of the following translators best illustrates the view described in the passage?
o: One who refuses to translate any text that contains a pun.
One who translates word for word so that nothing is lost.
One who keeps the formal tone of an official letter at the cost of some literal accuracy.
One who adds notes until every lost meaning is restored.
qs.e:
Evidence: the view is that translation is choosing which loss the reader can best afford. Keeping tone and giving up some literal accuracy is such a choice: (c).
Why not the others: (b) assumes nothing need be lost (opposite). (a) refusing is not choosing among losses (out of scope). (d) assumes every loss can be restored (opposite).
This is a stretch item: it asks you to apply the author's view to a new case, a step beyond the real paper's stems.
qs.p: Translation is commonly imagined as the transfer of a fixed meaning from one linguistic container to another, as though the sense of a sentence existed independently of the particular words that carry it. Experienced professional translators characteristically describe their activity rather differently, as a sequence of choices among losses: a pun can preserve its sound or its sense but rarely both, and a formal register in one language may have no counterpart in another that does not sound either stilted or casual. The question is seldom whether something will be lost, but which loss the reader of the translation can best afford.
